speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: DEATH OF FORMER PROVINCIAL PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister who has been confined to his bed for the last few days, I would like to say the following, on his behalf.
The death of Rene Levesque has affected me more than I can say. To a whole generation of Quebecers, including myself, Rene Levesque embodied the pride, the sense of belonging and the passion of Quebecers for their province.
From the dawn of the quiet Revolution to his retirement from political life, and during the May 1980 Referendum, Rene Levesque was the man of one dream and one cause: Quebec's full emancipation. During those years he took his province through some of the most difficult and at the same time most exhilarating times in its history.
Like all great politicians, Mr. Levesque was both a dreamer and a realist. He was able to make passion listen to reason. Whether or not all Canadians agreed with the cause for which he fought to the very end, they owe him this tribute: Rene Levesque was a great man and a great democrat.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: DEATH OF FORMER PROVINCIAL PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Quebec has just lost one of its most passionate sons and one of its most articulate spokesmen. Canada has lost a figure who dominated public life in this country and in his own province for nearly twenty years.
Rene Levesque embodied some of the characteristics of this country. His impatience, energy and compassion, his brillant discourse, his emotions, all will remain engraved in our memory as striking attributes of this remarkable man and his time.

For English Canadians he was that sometimes incorrigible man who would not let them forget his dream of a more sovereign Quebec.
I knew Rene Levesque. I had the honour to be the Parliamentary Secretary to the late Arthur Laing when he was Minister of Natural Resources of this country and Mr. Levesque was the Minister of Natural Resources. From 1963 on I enjoyed his company and the stimulating force of his personality. I did not share his vision of Quebec, nor his vision of Canada. But never once did I doubt his sincerity and his passionate commitment to the people of Quebec. Although he did not succeed in his ultimate quest, he forced Canada to come to terms with Quebec's place in Confederation under a renewed federalism. Rene Levesque was a man who reflected the spirit of Quebec and, in some ways, perhaps the spirit of Canada.

Rene Levesque's entire political career was a series of superlatives. He experienced great victories and great defeats. There was nothing ordinary about this man.
We remember the scenes of triumph on November 15, 1976. We remember the emotional atmosphere on both sides on the night of the Referendum in 1980.
Emotional and impatient though he was, Rene Levesque always set democracy above all other principles, and he always respected the democratic decisions made by Quebecers.
Mr. Speaker, speaking on behalf of the Liberal Party of Canada, we offer our sincere condolences to Rene Levesque's family and to all his friends.

subsubtopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE-FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare has the honour to present its first report. In accordance with its mandate under Standing Order 96(2), the committee agreed to study alcohol and drug abuse in Canada. The committee heard evidence from individuals and representatives of organizations in the field of addiction. It urges the Government to consider the recommendations contained herein.
Drug abuse in Canada is not a new problem. Last December when the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare began its study of drug abuse, there had been renewed concern by professionals and by ordinary Canadians about the abuse of drugs. A national poll that had recently been conducted indicated that the vast majority of Canadians believed that Canada had a serious problem of illicit drug use.
Following a meeting with the President of the United States, our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) called attention to this problem and began a governmental review process that resulted in $210 million in new federal Government initiatives under the national drug strategy.
The committee believed that it had an important role to play in providing advice to the House and to federal and provincial Governments on how best to address problems of substance abuse. Our work took us across Canada and brought us face to face with health care and social service professionals, government officials, citizen groups, young people, parents, and educators. We soon came to realize that substance abuse problems are not limited to the abuse of street drugs, but that Canada faces problems of the abuse of illicit drugs, legal overuse of prescription drugs and, above all, the abuse of alcohol.
Substance abuse problems are not limited to one part of Canada or one age group, but affect Canadians of all ages and walks of life in every province.
It is my pleasure to table in this House the first report of the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare entitled "Booze, Pills and Dope-Reducing Substance Abuse in Canada".
Our committee is recommending new initiatives with enhanced funding in prevention and treatment programs with a special emphasis on youth and aboriginal peoples. We are proposing steps to reduce the carnage on our highways caused by impaired drivers.
After careful review of the issue of substance abuse in the workplace, our committee is strongly opposed to the random testing of Canadian workers. We prefer to see a more cooperative and therapeutic approach to drug abuse in the workplace. Where drug testing is required because of real demonstrated risk to safety, we have recommended policies to provide safeguards.
Our committee wishes to see the federal Government discourage abusive drinking by maintaining an approach to taxation which recognizes the need to balance public health concerns with the overwhelming acceptance of social drinking by Canadians.
We are concerned that those who profit from the sale of alcoholic beverages shoulder their fair share of the responsibility to prevent alcohol abuse. Toward this end we are recommending that beverage alcohol advertisers be required to provide appropriate public education messages.
While the focus of the committee was on the health aspects of substance abuse, we also considered a number of measures related to the control of the supply of drugs. For example, we are recommending that federal and provincial Governments take steps to close "head shops", those businesses which specialize in the sale of drug paraphernalia. We would like to see law enforcement agencies given better tools to allow them to trace the profits of international drug trafficking.
Our committee has provided recommendations for the education of health care professionals, for program evaluation, and for the creation of a national centre on substance abuse. We realize that no matter what steps are introduced by Governments, there will always be some people who will abuse drugs. But we also believe that those recommendations, if implemented, will have a significant and positive effect on the reduction of substance abuse problems in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present the eleventh report of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts which deals with income tax expenditures.
November 2, 1987

The report particularly highlights the need for improved information to Parliament about tax expenditures, and the need for the Department of Finance to improve and put in place sound monitoring and evaluation procedures. Improvements are required both in the quality of tax expenditure information, and in the process whereby such information is provided to Parliament.
Income tax expenditures are demand driven, and by their nature may cost more than initially anticipated. Therefore, it is important that Parliament and the public be better informed about them.
The committee has recommended that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) table annual tax expenditure accounts in Parliament starting in 1987.
Pursuant to Standing Order 99(2) the committee has requested a comprehensive government response to certain recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, it is my duty to present a petition which is in accordance with Standing Order 106 and which relates to a sad situation concerning the broadcasting of Calgary's Winter Olympic Games, namely the fact that francophones outside Quebec will not have access to nation-wide French broadcasts. The situation is so serious, Mr. Speaker, that I have a number of petitions to present and I will be doing that this week with the support of my colleagues with a view to urging the Government and Radio-Canada to do something.
Mr. Speaker, close to one million francophones residing outside Quebec will not be able to watch French television broadcasts of the Calgary Olympic Winter Games.
Whereas the CRTC compromise under which French TV signals would be made available to cable companies is unacceptable because not all francophone communities outside Quebec have cable service; and whereas French-speaking Canadians will pay their share of the $200 million earmarked by the Conservative Government for the Calgary Winter Olympics Games organization, your petitioners humbly call upon Parliament to urge the Conservative Government to respect its commitments towards Canada's linguistic minorities by providing all communities from coast to coast with the possibility of watching, in both official languages, broadcasts of this international event, the 1988 Winter Olympics Games.
Petitions

Mr. Speaker, it is my duty to table a petition on behalf of residents of Shediac, St-Charles-de-Kent, Richibucto, Bass River, Rexton, Cap-Pele and Saint-Andre. Your petitioners deplore the fact that as part of its proposed tax reform, the Government is considering the possibility of putting a tax on food.
Wherefore, Mr. Speaker, your petitioners humbly pray Parliament to reject any measure that would have the effect of imposing a sales tax on food products.

Mr. Speaker, it is my duty to present a petition on behalf of constituents from the City of Thunder Bay and the Town of Red Rock who protest the changes made to the taxation system of Canada.
They protest that the tax reform proposals do not change an already unfair tax structure for average Canadian families, while wealthy Canadians earning over $100,000 per year do not pay their fair share and even receive a tax cut under the proposals.
They also protest the fact that 60,000 profitable corporations will be allowed to pay no income tax at all under the reform, and that the reform proposals include the possibility of a tax levy on food and other essential items.
They press for the restoration of full indexation in the personal tax system and urge the House of Commons to change these proposals of the Government.

Mr. Speaker, as I said a moment ago, I appreciate the opportunity to join in second reading debate on Bill C-87 which is designed to establish in Canada a harmonized tariff system. It is simply known as a system under which the movement of goods into and out of the country will be governed by a different classification system than the one that has prevailed for many years heretofore.
It is important that there be careful consideration of these matters. When we debate a Bill of this sort of course we are only dealing with the authorization. There are thousands of pages implementing a Bill of this sort-not that this one is
November 2, 1987

slight by itself-which can have far-reaching consequences on the industry. Therefore, I am pleased to take some time to debate it in order to raise appropriate questions about the implementation of the Bill, about its principles, perhaps even more so about the consequences of the Bill, and about questions of timing as to the carrying into effect of this change in classification.
I want to say at the outset that this is not a theoretical question at all. Questions have been raised and concern has been expressed by the Automotive Industries Association of Canada, which is a national trade organization of some 1,200 suppliers, distributors, and wholesalers of automotive parts, accessories, tools, and equipment. This industry employs over
70,000	people in Canada. It has a volume of sales which, at the wholesale level, exceed $7 billion. Members of the association are involved in extensive trade between Canada and the United States.
When an association of this sort raises questions about the timing of the proposal and expresses concern about the way the harmonized tariff system can impact on its operations, of which it is uncertain now, it seems to me it is important that Members of the House of Commons pay careful attention to it and to ensuring that this Chamber live up to its constitutional position as a deliberative chamber considering what may be the impact of the actions by the Canadian Government.
The proposal itself can have a good deal of practical value. We have all been aware in past months that the Canadian and American Governments have been working to ensure that their statistics on exports and imports are accurate. The figures released by the Americans on exports from Canada to the United States have sometimes been far larger than the Canadian figures and, if inaccurate, have served to feed the sense in the United States of being deluged by products from other countries. That could be very useful to arrive at a standard system of classification under which there can be no disagreement about the nature of the good and about the classification in the tariff system which should apply to it.
We have had a system of some 3,600 classifications. We now move from this end-use classification to another one in which the nature of the product itself will be the basis for classifying it. As the Automotive Industries Association has pointed out, where a rear view mirror for a motor vehicle was previously considered an automotive part, it will now simply be considered mirror glass. That sort of change, through one page after another of our tariff system, can have very important consequences for industries as it changes a particular tariff level that applies to a product.
The Government has been working on this change for seven years but the industry has only in the last months learned what the detailed nature of this system will be for each of the products produced it exports and it imports. To expect this system to be in effect as of January 1, 1988 rather than even a
Customs Tariff
few months later is rushing things. It begs the question whether the U.S. will have adopted the system by then or whether it will adopt it all. It imposes on the industry a discovery in practice of what the consequences will be as industry converts on the run rather than, having a good deal of lead time to consider the application and conceivably to reconsider purchase and sales practices. That seems to me to be a very important point to keep in mind.
I shall come back to it because this matter of how rapidly things are rushed through is something which concerns not only the Canadian tariff system and trade arrangements, but also the trade deal that is still being worked out with the United States. We were told it had been consummated a month ago, but we do not yet have the final details and we may well not have them much before the end of November. A committee will be voting on that end result early in December in order to allow a deadline in January. That sort of rushing of items is not carrying out the business of the country in a proper way.
There are some other concerns about the nature of the change which I want to put before the House this morning. The Automotive Industries Association has pointed out that to change from the previous end-use to a nature of item classification is not just a matter of doing things more accurately for classification purposes, it is not just a matter of arriving at a classification of our entire trade which will be in line with what is being done in the United States and other countries as well, it is not just a matter of ensuring that statistics are accurate, but it is a matter of far reaching consequences in the nature of the Auto Pact which governs trade between the two countries in automotive products.
Here we have a nice example of how pressing ahead on something which makes technical sense could have far reaching consequences. We have had understandings on where products should be made and how they should flow. We have had levels of Canadian content particularly established to protect industry in Canada. How will all of this impact on the new arrangements or, better put, what will the harmonized tariff system do to those arrangements?
I have been commenting on the speed with which all of this is being carried through. The proposal came to the industry very recently and there has been no opportunity to determine what its impact will be. The Versatile implements factory in Winnipeg had financial difficulties because of industry problems and because of problems experienced by its parent company in Vancouver, but this company was expecting to improve its productive facilities by bringing in welding equipment. This would have been possible under previous arrangements, but with the new changes in which it is classification by the nature of the product it will be impossible for Versatile to do so. This is a specific instance of a factory which should be improving its efficiency and productive potential being affected quite harmfully by this legislation.

The kinds of uncertainties I was feeling a few moments ago about information is, of course, integral to what we face with the trade deal supposedly concluded in early October. We were all given to understand that the agreement had been arrived at by Saturday night as the letter went over to the Capital buildings to assure members of Congress that a deal was in the bag. We have learned since then that negotiations went on through Sundary, that hard decisions still needed to be made and that those discussions were part of the difficulties in the different summaries that came out on the Sunday.
The U.S. summary clearly included items that were still on the American wish list. The Canadian summary was held back as Canadian negotiators fought for items which they wanted in the agreement and found difficulty in achieving. We had this picture late on a Sunday of the negotiators gathering before one of the Canadian representatives who had his documents in a briefcase on his lap. These were the documents that were to have been concluded the previous day. It presented a curious spectacle about which I am surprised American Congressmen have not made more. American Senators are still biding their time while lawyers for the Canadian and American Governments fight over the details to clarify the various arrangements of which we have only summaries now.
The pressure being placed on us here raises the possibility of far greater injury for the industries of Canada, for the regions of Canada and for the people of Canada than the Automotive Industries Association can raise in its own particular case. We will not have any real opportunity to debate the particulars when they finally appear. The committee will hardly have time to go into the details because we are bound to get an enormous document. I make no claim myself, much less than the industry does, to have looked at those 3,000 pages of the detailed changes which are being made.
This deal affects the whole trade of the country. Large industries which have previously not been affected by trade very much now find themselves having to worry about the consequences. To expect in a few days that we shall be able to come to grips and understand it is to expect a superhuman ability in this House of Commons which I have not seen. There is the possibility that a committee dominated by members of the Government will insist on ramming things through in just a few days at that point, as they were inclined to do when the committee began its hearings last week. It is certain that the people of Canada will not really have begun to understand fully the consequences of the deal by the time the committee has to vote on it.
Then there will be just days left for consideration of the deal in the House of Commons, at the same time as large items of other business including the various changes in taxation that were proposed last spring will have to be dealt with. This is not the way the business of Government should be done.
In recognizing the shortcomings of the Government's timetabling of these matters, one must also recognize that the fast-track proposal of the United States is one that has been imposed on us. Yet its consequences now are that the work continues when it was supposed to have been concluded. We expected surely that we would have three months to digest the deal. What we have instead is ongoing consideration of details.
We are told, in fact, not that this is all being resolved day by day as the discussions take place, but that disputes which will have to be resolved far above the level of lawyers for the two countries are being laid aside time after time. One can well imagine, on the precedent of the negotiations of that week or more at the end of September and the beginning of October through to a weekend-negotiations that turned out to take twice as long as we had initially thought they would-that this process will take time.
The worst of it is, as time becomes more and more difficult to find for all these deliberations, the Government sees only one hope for saving itself politically, and that is the possibility that enough Canadians may find this deal attractive at the end so they will vote for it and in the process vote for the Government. Here is a Government that knows it is finished in any other context, but this is its one hope. Is such a Government capable of the kinds of negotiations that are still clearly required?
It is not that matters were concluded at the beginning of October by any means. There are still all sorts of difficulties being raised. We know how good American lawyers and officials are at defending their own interests. Two sketches of the deal came out at the beginning of October and we have learned certain things about various areas from the summary. Its effect on the energy industries of the west is a lovely example of what caused the controversy that took place in the House last week.
We know, of course, that westerners want to export oil and gas and have often in the past experienced some difficulty entering the American market, but to get what they hope will be secure access, that magic phrase the Government holds out before us, what is the Government prepared to do but to yield its directing role in the industry. If the Canadian Government thought, in the case of another price inflation in energy, that it would be wise to try to hold back on the deal, there is no way that decision could be used by the Canadian Government to the advantage of Canadians. Surely the Americans would immediately demand that they have the same kind of access and that will surely make any kind of distinctive Canadian role in the energy industry at a time of great price increases very difficult.
What if petroleum feed stocks should be made available at a lower price than that which prevails in the market to a petrochemical company in Alberta in order to give it some advantage? Surely that will be protested immediately as an unfair subsidy. Any possibility that our resources might be used in a distinctive way to promote development in Canada,

even in cases where we do not think that we are providing any sort of unfair subsidy to industry, will be impossible.
Softwood lumber, of course, is a perfect example of that. Elere is a Government that negotiates politically and loses the battle. For government Members to protest that they are the ones defending western Canadian interests while we supposedly are not is to try to make the same kind of argument they would want to make against the automotive industries which is that they have safeguarded the interests of the industry. However, the industry says that they have not, that more time is needed for careful consideration of the harmonized tariff system. The industry needs to be sure of what its consequences are and I call on the Government to ensure that it has enough time to do that.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-87. I do not intend to take my full 20 minutes because there are only a few points that I want to make.
Bill C-87, as has already been explained by the previous speaker, is largely a technical Bill. It provides for a new customs classification system which is due to take effect on January 1, 1988. I would like to speak at the outset about the process because I think the process at this point in time is just as important as the Bill itself.
I refer to the process because there has been voiced already by a major component of the Canadian industrial sector an opposition, not so much to the substance or total content of the Bill but to the fact that this Bill has come on rather quickly and is being, not rammed through Parliament but debated in rather short order, even though seven years of investigation and research has gone into it. Certain components of the industrial sector seem to feel that they have not had sufficient time to study all the details of this very technical Bill.
I refer specifically, of course, to the auto parts industry which has already made representation to the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin). It would like the effective date of the legislation date put back from January 1 to April 1, 1988, to give it greater time to study the full impact of this Bill, the major purpose of which is to harmonize the tariff system as it presently exists between the United States and Canada.
The reason I am concerned about process here is because, as other speakers have alluded to and very appropriately, this kind of process with inadequate consultation or lead time for thorough discussion and understanding of the item being debated is very directly related to the totally unacceptable process of the debate on free trade. I suggest that that is related to Bill C-87, and certainly for purposes of debate in this Chamber.

I think it is absolutely unacceptable that a standing committee should be charged with the awesome responsibility of thoroughly investigating the advantages and disadvantages or content of a memorandum of agreement without actually having the opportunity to spend several weeks, indeed even several months, digesting, discussing, debating and trying to understand the content of the actual finished agreement. This is the responsibility we have placed on the shoulders of the House Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade.
I suggest that the basic reason why last week there was so much heated debate, name-calling and personalization of a legislative process, why individual Ministers were criticized and condemned, why Members of Parliament were hurling unacceptable language back and forth at each other, both in the House and in committee, is because we did not have a finished document to debate. Consequently, and I am speaking now from an Opposition point of view, they had to direct their attack not against a Bill, resolution, or some kind of finished document, but against the process.
Your Honour, you sat on this side of the House for many years, as have many of your colleagues in the Government. You and they know that when you do not have the finished product to debate you end up directing your fire, your wrath, your criticism at the process. That is what is happening today on this issue of free trade.
For the life of me, I cannot imagine a U.S. Senate committee debating a proposed treaty between the U.S. and a foreign country without having a copy of that treaty in their hands. It would be anathema to the American congressional system.
This is one of the fundamental weaknesses of this Chamber. I am not pointing a finger at any one Minister or any one Government. We are all to some extent to blame. This is a legislature. It is also part of the executive branch. We have to clearly define and delineate the responsibilities of the legislative branch and the executive branch. If the Government expects us on this side of the House to intelligently and knowledgeably debate such an important matter as the free trade agreement, then we must demand a finished copy of the agreement with all the i's dotted and all the t's crossed. Unfortunately, we do not have that document.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in this debate on harmonization. I think many Canadians do not even know what harmonization means, including many Members of the House. That has been clear from the quality of the debate we just heard from the Minister. Obviously he is not interested in dealing with this issue.
The Bill itself seeks to bring about an international standard which would expedite trading among GATT nations. That is laudable and something we support. We in the Liberal Party believe strongly in liberalized trade, in reaching out to all parts of the world. However, I have some concerns, and I think they have been articulated by some of the other Hon. Members who have spoken.
Let us look at what will happen with harmonization between Canada and the United States under the free trade deal. 1 come from the Niagara region of the country, the Golden Horseshoe as it is known, the area which, along with British Columbia, produces fruits and grapes. As a result of the free trade deal, our grape industry will be wiped out as of next year. Ontario wine companies have already told the grape producers that they will not buy their 1988 crop because they will bring grapes in from the United States more cheaply, specifically grapes to be used for the production of table wine.
However, Canadians also eat table grapes. I just became aware, by examining some of the issues surrounding free trade, that in the United States they spray table grapes with sulphur so that they will last longer. As well, sulphur kills the cocoon eggs of fruit flies. Because the Americans want to sell grapes to Canada and other places they are concerned about fruit flies and so spray them with sulphur, but such spraying is not legal in Canada. We do not permit farmers to spray their grapes with sulphur because it could present a potential health hazard.
The reason I am raising this is that if we harmonize with the United States in entering into free trade, will we harmonize to the high Canadian standard which does not permit the spraying of sulphur on table grapes, or will we harmonize to the lowest common denominator, the American standard, which allows the spraying of grapes with sulphur?
Just a few days ago I was speaking with the Minister of the Environment for the Province of Ontario about some issues with which many Canadians are only just now beginning to come to grips. This is one of the reasons why we should have a full and open debate on all of the elements of free trade.

Mr. Speaker, unemployment in the construction industry on Cape Breton Island is unacceptably high. The Cape Breton Building and Construction Trades Council has concluded that a government program designed to provide a program for older worker adjustment would be most appropriate for the workers represented by the Council.
Since the relative boom years of the late 1960s and early 1970s, when union membership was 25 per cent higher than the present levels, employment prospects for workers in the construction industry in Cape Breton have been bleak.
Many of the 4,500 workers represented by the 14 unions affiliated with the Cape Breton Building and Construction Trades Council have been forced by economic conditions to lead a "merry-go-round" existence which sees them repeating a cycle of short term employment, unemployment insurance, welfare, short term employment, and so on.
At the present time 25 per cent of union members are employed, leaving 3,375 unemployed.
The inevitable consequences of these unstable and marginal employment prospects include stress, ill-health and family breakdown.
I call on the Government of Canada to implement the program it announced several years ago with regard to older workers' adjustment. Stop negotiating with the provinces and start providing some action for older workers.

subtopic: POSITION OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY ON NATO AND FREE TRADE
POSITION OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY ON NATO AND FREE TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Members of the "New Socialist Party" of Canada are acting like lemmings, blindly following ideology and policies which are archaic and myopic regarding the future of Canada.
The New Democrats should take time to examine the record of other socialist Governments. Take NATO and free trade. The NATO Alliance was created by a group of nations, many of which were socialist. When the EEC was created, almost half the countries had socialist Governments. It is very evident that these socialist countries placed the well-being of their people in the forefront.
The point is very simple. NATO is there to ensure that our democratic system of government continues to survive. The European Community realized very early that trade barriers would inhibit their nations' economic growth and hurt their people. They found that when they lowered the trade barriers the distinct European societies, both large and small, were not threatened. Cultural identities, monetary policies, armed forces, and government, all continue to function as before. The only thing that changed was how their people benefited from the improved economic climate.
The NDP should look at the EEC's economic success instead of listening to the Bob Whites of the world whose interests are very narrow. Free trade will give Canada a very healthy future.
In agreeing to this type of non-reciprocal elimination of trading advantages, the Government has once again failed to act in the best interest of Canada's agricultural producers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Abraham Lincoln once said: "God must have loved the plain people: He made so many of them". The plain people mentioned by Lincoln are the rank and file, the ordinary people, the workers.
Today I want to talk about the plain people. I believe I can speak for them because I am one of them. Common people have a tough time making both ends meet. They are not flush with this world's goods and many live from hand to mouth. Any reduction in the things they have to buy is a godsend. That is why free trade is attractive to the rank and file. Most, if not all, of the things they buy will be cheaper under free trade.
It will be a bonanza for the young couple planning marriage, as washing machines, dishwashers, bed sheets, furniture, et cetera will save them a lot of dollars. There will be jobs, and opportunities to advance as Canadians as we will lose no sovereignty.
Free trade will open the doors to a whole new world for Canada and Canadians. That is why the PC Party is fighting the Liberals, the New Democrats and the leaders of the trade unions. We want the workers to have a future, a great future. Free trade can give it to them.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in debate on Bill C-87 which is a Bill respecting the imposition of customs and other charges. The Bill has to do with providing relief against the imposition of certain duties. By this Act we are revising our present and very complex system of describing and coding commodities that go into international trade. It has been well documented for a long while that goods often fall into more than one of these categories. That, of course, causes confusion and does not help in attaining what we all want, that is, fair and easier multinational trade.
It should be noted that Bill C-87 is part of a multilateral agreement that was worked out among the EEC countries, the United States of America, Japan, and Canada. Work on the revision of this complicated code began in Canada in 1981. The actual international negotiations began in October of 1986, and the changes that we have in Bill C-87 were negotiated with Canada's trading partners which belong to the General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs.
What will Bill C-87 do for the country? What will it do for our exporters and our importers? It will make it easier for them to classify goods. It will reduce the number of classification appeals which are always expensive and time consuming. Of course, no one in the world of business is particularly keen on a great deal of government red tape. Therefore, the passage of this Bill should make it easier to do business and trade with the European Economic Community, Japan and our largest
Customs Tariff
and most important of all trading partners, that is, the United States of America.
It is almost unnecessary for anyone to say that Canada is a trading nation, but recognizing that fact is absolutely essential in understanding our national economy. Our prosperity depends essentially on how much of our goods and services we can sell throughout the world, whether it is in Europe, Asia- including the market in China which is opening up-Latin America or the United States.
Interestingly enough, our exporters do not have to work quite as hard at finding a market in the United States as they do in some parts of the world.
It has become very easy for us to do business with the Americans. While I could be challenged on this observation, I believe that sometimes it has led to a certain laziness or lack of ambition of some exporters to try to find those more difficult markets abroad.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that wonderful occasion when I was under your leadership on a very important visit to the People's Republic of China. You may recall that questions were raised with the delegation about why our business people in Canada were not more energetic. We were asked why they do not try harder when there are business opportunities for them in China.
We were told that the Chinese like Canada because of what it did a long while ago in leading the western world in the recognition of the legitimacy of the Chinese Government. We were asked why Canadian businessmen did not take advantage of that fact.
That is a good question and one that I cannot answer. Perhaps a clue lies in the fact that we have had it so easy both in the past and in the present in doing business with the United States that we do not try harder in some other parts of the world.
This afternoon we are debating the principle of Bill C-87. It seems to me that the principle is basically sound. First, it is that multilateral trade is essential because we in Canada, as trading nation, would never want to put ourselves in a position of being locked into doing business with a single customer.
I suggest that anyone in business would be just a little worried if their goods were sold to one buyer. If that customer decided to operate differently, what would become of the supplier?
It is always healthier to diversify, and the approach Canada must take is to trade as widely as possible throughout the world and leave no potential market unexploited. We have good products to sell and there are good business people in this country. We do not want to miss any area of the world where a Canadian product could be provided.

Customs Tariff
The easier and freer the trade in most cases, the better it is for Canada. I recognize, however, that there are certain circumstances where certain regions of the country with a certain product at a certain time may require a degree of protection. However, it should always be emphasized to those people that the protection must be temporary in nature as a means to become established. It should not be regarded as a permanent government protection.
We are beginning a national debate on a new trade deal between Canada and the United States. A number of questions can be asked about this agreement which I believe relate directly to the principle of the Bill before us. There are questions that I want to pose: Does the new trade agreement that has been negotiated with the United States really provide freer and easier access to the U.S. market? Does it really save us from the threat of U.S. protectionism which is growing and causing a good deal of concern in our country? Does it really give us any greater and wider access to the U.S. market than we have now? Does it mean that our tremendous trade surplus with the United States will become still greater?
As I listen to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promote the deal that he and his officials negotiated, I get the idea that our multi-billion dollar trade surplus-which I believe to be in the neighbourhood of $20 billion-will perhaps double. While I have not heard that exact prediction, it is the impression I get from listening to what has been promised. There will be an increase in the trade surplus and there will be more direct jobs as a result.
I want to make some preliminary comments on the initial transcript of the elements of a Canada-U.S. agreement. That is all we can do since we do not yet have the details. I suggest that everything to be said about this agreement must be preliminary in nature.
First, the debate that is beginning to take shape will feature a number of leading characters in this country, including economists, academics, politicians, trade unionists, people from the business sector, agriculture and so on. It should be very clear that what we are debating in Canada is not free trade versus protectionism. If the debate is nothing else than that, I suggest that it will be a futile effort, largely a waste of time. While such a debate will stir the emotions on each side of the question, I do not think much will be accomplished.
It is generally agreed that freer and easier trade is better than locking ourselves into an isolationist cell. That would be absurd and could hardly be the subject of any kind of debate. Therefore, the debate in Canada should not be the highly academic one of free trade versus protectionism. That should be left for an assignment we might very well give to a first-year class in economics. But that is not the issue in this debate.
The real debate is the Canada-U.S. trade agreement that has been negotiated, what exists now, and what we could have if a better agreement had been negotiated. The questions we must ask are: For whom is this trade agreement good, for
whom is it not so good, and for whom is it downright dangerous and even damaging?
It is extremely difficult to speak definitively on this issue because we do not have all the details of the agreement. It seems to me rather premature for a Commons committee to begin an intensive study and analysis since we need the details in order to do that. We want to debate the question in terms of what is known. We do not want the debate to be hysterical in nature, we want it to be informed and balanced.
I suggest that once we have the full agreement, it is then vital and quite necessary that all the time necessary be set aside to see whether or not we have a good agreement. In other words, a timetable, a time restriction of a few weeks or a few months cannot be put on it. Let us have enough time. If we are doing something as important for the future of our nation as this trade agreement may be, we need time to consider for whom it will be detrimental and in what ways. Whose wellbeing will it contribute to in the economic terms of our nation? What threats are there, if any, to our sovereignty, to our political independence?
As we are drawn deeper and deeper into the U.S. economy acted out on the stage of a North American continentalism, what will be the benefits for Canada? What will be the gains and the losses? Surely, to raise those questions is in no way to be unfair to the Government. To raise those questions, it seems to me, is the responsibility of every citizen. It certainly is the responsibility of those who are elected to represent our citizens in the House of Commons. So each sector and each Canadian interest must carefully examine for itself or have done for it how the U.S.-Canada trade agreement will impact upon it.
The grape growers, for example, are concerned. Are their concerns legitimate? Are they well based in reality and in fact? The automobile workers are worried about the effects on the Auto Pact which has benefited them with secure jobs, in most cases, and reasonable benefits for the work they do. Canadians wonder whether our financial institutions will face the possibility of U.S. takeovers. If they are taken over by U.S. interests, what will this do to our banking system? Will it improve it or will it be detrimental to the banking system? Will we lose control if we no longer have the financial institutions under our jurisdiction fully and totally? Will somehow our economic control be diminished at the same time?
The agricultural critics on this side of the House have raised many important questions and concerns. They need to be answered. The Premier of Ontario and his Government are apprehensive, to put it mildly, about the possible effects of this Canada-U.S. trade agreement on a very healthy Ontario economy.
The list is a long one. But coming as I do from northern Ontario, which is a resource region of this country, I have some questions that my constituents are putting to me,
November 2, 1987

questions that need answers. Let me say at the beginning that I do not in any way fear a policy which gives the Americans the first option on the buying of Canadian resources. If they buy those resources which, first of all, we have all determined are excess to our domestic needs, and we have set them aside for export purposes to be purchased at fair market value by the Americans, our good friends, our friends with whom we are aligned internationally and in terms of defence arrangements, then to give them first option is not repugnant to me at all. It makes perfectly good sense. But when we do that, can we be assured by the Government in this debate that there will be no resource grabs?
What do I mean by that? Can we have the assurance that, if there is unrestricted investment from the United States in the development of our resources, we will still be able to control our own resource policy? Will we still be able to make those decisions that this amount of our resources is surplus, eligible for export, can be sold at a fair price, and the Americans can have first option? Can we have that assurance?
We in northern Ontario in recent years have been the beneficiaries of free trade. We have, for example, had free trade in pulp, paper, lumber and minerals. It was only in the 1980s that we were suddenly shocked, as if a pail of cold water had been thrown on our heads, by the U.S. countervail action on our softwood lumber. We fought and we won that action in the United States once before, before the International Trade Commission. It was expensive. It was time consuming. The Liberal Government of the day stood behind the industry and we were victorious. We thought that that was the end of it. But during this administration, countervail action, again from the U.S. coalition of lumber producers, has come forward, and this time for reasons that are still inexplicable to me. There was no fight in us. We could not stand up to the United States of America. We buckled under, and instead of going ahead with the countervail action and seeing if we could win it-and the chances were good that we would win-we gave in. We imposed upon ourselves, something very curious for a trading nation, a 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), under questioning in this House, justified it by saying, "Well, at least we are keeping the money in the country". That is true enough. But that export tax has forced marginal operations to close. Four sawmills in my constituency were forced to close directly because of the 15 per cent. It is true that they were not big profit earners, but they were making their own way. They were providing jobs, and four of them closed. Another one that was scheduled to open never did. Therefore, the total is five.
With respect to the trade deal, the first question that I ask and the first telephone calls that I got from northern Ontario were to this effect. What does the new Canada-U.S. trade deal do for the 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber? Here is the answer. The answer is that that arrangement is now locked into the agreement forever and a day. The parties have agreed that the free trade agreement does not impair or prejudice the exercise of any rights or enforcement measures arising out of
Customs Tariff
the 1986 softwood lumber memorandum of understanding. So an agreement that we thought was going to give us free trade in northern Ontario, that was going to give us relief from a 15 per cent export tax, we realize now is with us for all time to come.
Some very good analysis has been done on the free trade agreement. The Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) said to me in answer to questions, "If we had had this new arrangement, if we had had this new binational panel in effect, then the problems that you had in northern Ontario, in B.C., the Maritime provinces and Atlantic Canada with the softwood lumber you would not have". A very reputable firm by the name of Osier, Hoskin & Harcourt has come to this conclusion with regard to the new trade arrangement:
If these rules had been in effect at the time of last year's U.S. subsidy case against exports of Canadian softwood lumber, the mechanism proposed under the agreement would not have led to any different result for Canadian exporters than that which occurred.
So the question that my constituents are asking is this. What have we gained for softwood lumber under this agreement? I have to tell them that we have not gained anything. All we have done now is to have carved it in stone. It is there as part of an international agreement for all time to come.
You are indicating, Mr. Speaker, that I have very little time left. I just want to raise one other question. It has to do with where decisions will be made in the future. In British Columbia, the Government has tried to replace the 15 per cent tax with a higher stumpage fee. What they have ended up with is paying the higher stumpage fee plus the 15 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Forestry and Mines)
speechtext: Temporarily!

That is right. Instead of paying $5 a thousand board feet to produce it, they are temporarily paying between $80 and $90. My hon. friend opposite was quite right to interject with "temporarily". Why. is it temporary? Why cannot the Minister for International Trade go to the United States and say, "You have raised your stumpage fees in British Columbia therefore you have a clean bill of health with respect to the 15 per cent export tax"? What she said to the industry was this. "First, I must clear it with Washington". The Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) said the same thing in another respect. The Council of Forest Ministers in Canada has agreed that there can be a system of provincial levies to replace the 15 per cent export tax. They have gone to the Minister and said, "Here is our proposal". The Minister said, "On paper it looks good. But first of all I have to see if Washington and the U.S. lumber industry will say that it is adequate and it fulfils what they see as being necessary".
I wish to say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the House that there is a warning here for all of us. It looks to me as if the Canada-U.S. trade agreement will mean that more and more decisions that affect various commodities and various aspects of our economy will first have to be cleared by Washington.

November 2, 1987
Customs Tariff
That worries me. It seems to me that that is a definition of having our sovereignty threatened. It does seem to me that we are losing our political independence. This is only a small signal. Perhaps it is only a little storm on the horizon. I wish to know, is that small storm going to be a full-blown tempest? If it is, Sir, on every side of the House and from every region of this country we all ought to be seriously concerned. We need to know the answers before we say yes to the Americans on this U.S.-Canada trade agreement that has been negotiated.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-87 before us today could be described as customs harmonization legislation. I imagine that, from the government side, it is a very routine and technical matter as it has been put forward. In reality, it is a matter of serious concern to Canadians.
It is interesting, when we go back in history, that the Customs Tariff has been an extremely important instrument of national and industrial policy in Canada. If my memory serves me correctly, the Customs Tariff, much the same as we see it in the format today, was inaugurated during the time of Sir John A. Macdonald under the national policy.
In those days the Conservatives had a national view of Canada. Indeed, Confederation was an attempt to unite the provinces of British North America against absorption by the United States. In those days the Conservatives had a vision of Canada. The Customs Tariff when it was developed in the national policy was part of this vision.
In order to prevent Canada from simply being a hewer of wood and carrier of water, the Conservative Government of the day imposed a Customs Tariff which forced American producers not only to export to Canada and totally overwhelm Canadian industry, but to develop industry in Canada in order to manufacture here, create employment, add value to the resources of this country, enrich people, and strengthen Canada.
That is a thumb-nail sketch of what the Conservative Party was formerly. It was nationalist, it developed Confederation, it developed a national industrial policy, and the Customs Tariff formed an integral part of that. It was absolutely opposed to free trade with the United States. It had a sense of long vision, and it knew what would be the end result of free trade with the Americans, with unimpeded access to the full Canadian market. It knew that we would be destroyed economically and industrially, and Canadian sovereignty would be gone.
It is interesting to see the complete reversal of roles as the modern-day Conservative Government for short-term alleged benefit would see Canada overwhelmed by the United States. The elephant and the mouse image is very clear that Canada will be overwhelmed by the United States. Today the Conservative Government does not have a national vision of Canada. It sees an integrated market, almost a great big North American cash register. It does not see the preservation of Canada as a major priority from an economic viewpoint,
and as that economic absorption occurs, certainly Canadian sovereignty will be lost. What we are looking at is far more that the economic amalgamation in Europe in the European Economic Community where in many cases partners are reasonably balanced and protective mechanisms are in place. With the over-hasty agreement, the enormous concessions, and the failure to develop the concept of what trade improvements with the United States should be, this Government has sold Canada down the river economically, and Canadian sovereignty will be gone if this deal moves forward.
My colleagues to the right in the Liberal Party, the old Grits of Canadian history, were free traders. It is interesting to see them wrap themselves in sheep's clothing today and stand up as opponents and spokespersons for Canadian nationalism and Canadian ownership and direction when, in fact, the Liberal Party of old was a Party of free traders. The present Leader of this Party, the Right Hon. Member who represents the riding of Vancouver Quadra from Toronto, wrote in a book not too many years ago that Canada should be seeking wide open free trade with the United States. In that same book, he indicated that the manner to entice Americans into such a free trade agreement was a give away of resources. He specifically mentioned a give away of water in the literature.
One must be very cautious. As ordinary Canadians watching the unfolding of the political drama over free trade in Ottawa, on the one hand we see that Conservatives, who used to be nationalists with a vision of Canada and a sense of responsibility to protect the Canadian economy, develop it, watch it flourish, and protect Canadian sovereignty, have now switched to being Liberals, free traders. On the other hand, the Liberals, who used to be free traders, are now telling us that they are Conservatives and that they have a vision of Canada. All this stems from the Customs Tariff, the proper development of it and using it to shape the operation of the Canadian economy.
During the period when the Liberals were in power, they recognized the complete sell-out of Canada in the sense that under their administration eventually they watched Americans come and obtain almost unrestricted acquisition of Canadian industry and the Canadian economy.
I recall reading at one time that Alastair Gillespie, when he was Minister of Energy, was asked in the House if there was any protection, any monitoring of American acquisition of Canadian industries. He stated, "Well, no, there is no formal one. My secretary, if she happens to see a clipping in a newspaper or magazine that is interesting, will clip it out and call it to my attention, but that is all the monitoring that goes on".
The end result of that type of attention from our free trading friends in the Liberal Party was that Canada lost a great deal of its sovereignty. We watched Americans come into this country, pick off a Canadian company that was competing in this market with them, and buy it, then they would shut it down. The operation would be served from the United States.
November 2, 1987

The Americans would come in to a Canadian company that was exporting overseas, doing the type of research, marketing, and innovative business activities that were required to make Canada a great nation to expand our export capabilities, and state that that company was competing with them. There was no restriction. They would buy the company and shut it down, or else they would insist that it serve only the Canadian market while the American parent company served the international exports. This is all part of the record. It is part of the history of the Liberal Party, and indeed also part of the Conservative history in Canada. It is well documented and absolutely true.
By unlimited investment in Canada, the Americans were able to shut down vigorous Canadian companies and provide the product from the United States. They were able to shut down vigorous Canadian companies that exported abroad, take those exports and insist that they be done from the United States and that the Canadian company, using U.S. parts, assemble a product in Canada and serve the Canadian market with it.
We do not have any serious misunderstanding about the intention of the Conservatives in this regard. Under the free trade agreement they have completely opened up foreign investment in Canada. The end result will be just as I have said-the Americans will come in now that customs tariffs will be removed, will buy Canadian companies, and will shut them down. That employment will go to the United States. American companies will shut down vigorous Canadian companies which are exporting products overseas. They will limit their activities to the Canadian market, force them into assembly operations rather than development, and indeed put an end to vigorous Canadian competition overseas.
It is a matter of size. Canadian banks have played an enormous role in this regard. It is well documented. Canadian banks would rather lend money to large U.S. multinational firms than they would to Canadian entrepreneurs, basically because of the large sack of cash on which American companies are sitting. American companies would not have to put up any cash to buy out Canadian companies. In fact, Canadian banks would be quite prepared to lend them the money to take over Canadian companies and to sell the soul of Canada for a small cut of interest from a secure borrower in the United States. The banks of Canada assisted the undoing of the nation in terms of foreign investment.
It goes even further. What about when the United States was plagued with balance of payments problems? We should be looking at the kinds of services allowed into the country. During the periods of Nixon and Johnson, they both encouraged American multinational companies to come to Canada and remove profits rather than invest them here. They were told to remove the profits and to sell services to their wholly owned subsidiaries. They were to sell legal services from American law firms, not from Canadian ones. It involved the whole range of services used by industry-engineering,
Customs Tariff
research, and advertising. It was almost an American policy to redress its balance of payments during the Vietnam War. It forced branch plants in Canada to acquire all their services to whatever degree they could in the United States in order to ensure that the money flowed out of Canada and did not wind up in the pockets of Canadian service organizations, consultants, engineers, researchers, lawyers, or accountants. Those professional groups watched as the money flowed across the border and into the United States.
What we have before us today is a Conservative Government advocating not only that that happen but that the whole process be accelerated. It is absolutely dishonest.
I imagine that the Government will roam the country telling Canadians that the free trade agreement is a good operation in its present form. More and more Canadians are coming to understand that the unbridled ability of American companies to come into Canada, to purchase Canadian firms, and to do what they will with them, will mean that in the end Canada will not be a sovereign nation. We will not be able to control our economy. Under the Liberal regime we came very close to losing the ability to direct it. With the free trade agreement before us there is no doubt that we will see the loss of the ability of the Canadian Government and of the Canadian people to direct our economy.
It is astounding that we sit here juggling customs duties today without any intention to develop a national policy behind them but simply to accommodate Americans. I challenge Conservative Members to rise in the House and tell us in what way this will assist the Canadian economy to grow. In what way will Canadian business and industry grow from this particular manoeuvre? The honest answer is that they will not. It will simply facilitate the process of the Americanization of Canada.
It is interesting that no one can deny the kinds of things which brought into place the Foreign Investment Review Act, as weak an instrument as it was. It was almost an invitation to American firms to invest in Canada. The Liberals refused to put real teeth in it. They always did things half measure. They never really knew whether they were Liberals or Conservatives when it came to confronting issues. As a result, there was never direction in the country. There was always lip service paid to serious problems. Indeed the Foreign Investment Review Act was merely lip service. It should have been much tighter.
They also constantly refused to develop a national industrial policy. In the absence of a national industrial policy, the Foreign Investment Review Act was out in limbo trying to manage investment without any idea or any picture of what they wanted the economy to be or to do. Unfortunately that was the supreme failure of the previous Government. It had no idea. It had no sense of Canada. It had no view of Canada as a nation. That could have come from a national industrial strategy. However, the major flaw today is that the Conservative Government, in much the same way as did the Liberals, is

November 2, 1987

approaching free trade in a manner which will leave Canadians severely handicapped. It has no picture of what the Canadian economy should look like. There is no industrial strategy in Canada to help Canadian industrialists and entrepreneurs to strengthen themselves and be able to compete effectively in the United States market. Only the losers have been highlighted. Some 300,000 to 500,000 people could lose their jobs. There could be massive dislocation.
On the other side of the coin there is the hope that some businesses will be able to export across the line. Such businesses will find severe competition from much larger corporations with much more money to come into Canada. They will not only be denied access into the United States, but they will be put out of business in the Canadian market.
Let us look at the American view of this particular treaty, the one which they will use as argument in the United States to sell the agreement. Anyone in the United States who sits down and reads the agreement will be absolutely thrilled. There will be a rush to support it because it is such a massive giveaway of this country.
To some degree the softwood lumber problem is a red herring. I think that the Conservative Government, in conjunction with the provinces, has already worked out a solution. Of course it is the right of the Canadian Government to remove the export tax. I suspect that that would come very close to the time of the agreement. When many people in Canada are hollering that it is flawed only because of the softwood lumber agreement, the Government will simply whip it away and say that it has solved all their problems. In fact that is likely to happen on that particular issue.
However, a really tragic aspect of the particular agreement is the ability of the United States to buy out Canada, to come in and purchase competitive firms, to limit their capacity if not close them, and to apply without any sanction whatsoever the old bogyman of the extraterritorial application of the U.S. law in Canada. An absolutely wide open opportunity has been given to exercise that in Canada, far worse than ever before.
It is astounding to know what are the benefits of the agreement. It certainly seems that the primary concerns are loss of Canadian sovereignty, the deindustrialization of Canada, and the ownership of the major percentage of what industry exists being in the hands of the United States.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Comox- Powell River (Mr. Skelly) was talking about deindustrialization of Canada. My concern is about the need for developing industrialization in the part of Canada from which he and I come. The whole Province of British Columbia and, indeed, western Canada, is based on resources. The classic idea is that through exporting resources there would be an accumulation of capital, which would then be used to develop secondary industry. That is the justification for developing and exploiting resources at a very rapid rate. That has not happened in
British Columbia or in other parts of western Canada largely because the head offices of the companies exploiting the resources are not situated in the West. They are in eastern Canada or are multinationals located in Chicago, New York or wherever.
Given the free trade agreement, given the difficulty that we have already in trying to develop secondary industry,what will happen to the possibility of developing secondary industry in the communities which the Member represents on Vancouver Island, and what about the mainland?

Mr. Speaker, to answer the very perceptive question from the Hon. Member for Cowichan, Malahat and The Islands (Mr. Manly) let me quote some of the most distinguished Members of the House of Commons today. I am quoting directly from Maclean's magazine for June 13, 1983. The now Secretary of State (Mr. Clark) said:
Unrestrained free trade with the United States raises the possibility that thousands of jobs could be lost in such critical industries as textiles, furniture and footwear. Before we jump on the bandwagon of continentalism, we should strengthen our industrial structure so that we are more competitive.
That is what I tried to put forward to the House today. The now Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie), at that time a leadership candidate, said:
It's silly. Canada must improve relations and trade with the United States, of course. But our natural destiny is to become a global leader, not America's weak sister.
That is absolutely what I said a few minutes ago.
John Gamble, a notable Canadian who found succour in the arms of the Conservative Party, said:
We would be eaten alive. If we opened our market to the United States, we won't be able to sustain our manufacturing.
That is one of the very few times in my life that I have agreed with John Gamble.
Then the now Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said about free trade:
Canadians rejected free trade with the United States in 1911. They would do so again in 1983. Canada must increase its share of the total world trade, which has dropped by 33 per cent in the past two decades.
What can I say? What happened to him today?
Peter Pocklington, another one who has found warmth and comfort in the bosom of the Conservative Party, said:
1 believe in free trade between Canada and the United States, but we must ensure that Canadian industry gets the same access as we give the Americans.
He is one of the true. I think a Liberal moved over there. Then we have the now Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) who said:
Bilateral free trade with the United States is simplistic and naive. It would only serve to further diminish our ability to compete internationally.
With such noted Canadians standing up and appealing for support within their own Party and to the nation as a whole for their view of what a stupid idea free trade is, what can I say?
November 2, 1987

Mr. Speaker, I do respect many of the ideas of the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway) and respect the distinguished service he has given in the House, but on free trade I think he has been misled.
If you look at the European Economic Community, many partners are of similar size with balanced economies. If we were 250 million people strong we would be looking at a more open trade arrangement with the United States. The dilemma is that we are 25 million people as opposed to 250 million and we will be overwhelmed, just as the candidates for the leadership and his own Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said in the past.
Second, the free trade agreement before us today is a rush job. There is no protection in the agreement. If you read the briefing notes put forward by the United States administration to convince the Senate and the Congress to support this, the Americans believe that Canadians have sold themselves out, that it is a deal too good to pass up. In the minds of many Canadians the Conservative Government has made this its sole reason for existence, and it is the entire issue before this Parliament. In order to get the agreement through in a timely manner, the Government had to rush it to the point where the Canadian Government was not able to build things that strengthen Canada allowing us to compete effectively, namely, a gradual opening up of certain trade sectors, such as the automobile sector.
The Government opposite has spoken about the Auto Pact as an example of free trade. But we had sector trade liberalization which enabled us to develop a small section of the economy in a more effective way. However, it took a considerable period of time to do it, and has been under way for a period of time with plenty of safeguards for Canada. That does not exist in the free trade agreement. It throws off all control by Canada and the ability to direct the economy. It gives an invitation to the United States to come here and take the country over.

Mr. Speaker, I found the comments by my friend, the Hon. Member for Comox- Powell River (Mr. Skelly) very interesting. I taught Canadian history at the university before I was elected to Parliament in 1984. I find the shifts in attitudes and the change of position of the Conservative Party and this Government of ours truly astonishing. The Member sketched quite well the attitude that used to exist and the position which the present Government is taking. The Member spot-lighted that change in attitude by giving us the excerpts which Maclean's magazine published in 1983 during the leadership race of the Conservative Party and the position the various candidates took. The only one who came close to supporting the stand of the present Government was Mr. Pocklington from Edmonton. Yet, this is a Government in which various of these candidates are front-bench Members, one of whom, having won the leadership and having taken a very critical stance, has suddenly become the wildest partisan of this continental trade arrangement with the United States, the continental union of 100 years ago which was rejected by Conservatives at that time. The Liberals realized the political foolishness of it fairly quickly. They came up with a different refinement.
What explanation does my friend have for this? I realize that this tests all of our comprehensions when we see this kind of watershed change in attitude. What was it that led the Prime Minister and his colleagues to take such a stand and get into this continental deal with the United States over the last two years or so?

Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to cast our minds backwards for some of the answers in the historical fabric of Canada. I would bow to the expertise of the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) into whose field I am treading. I would not mind if I could reverse the question and have him talk to us a little bit about the annexation manifesto which generated from a large number of Conservatives and downtown Montreal businessmen. At that particular time in 1849, they were quite prepared to sign the whole country over and get themselves annexed to the United States. I am afraid today that this particular agreement is the same kind of an expression, an annexation manifesto that will tie us to the United States. In that tying, the United States, with a much larger population, 10 times that of Canada, will overwhelm this country.
I think the critical point is that leaping into an agreement with the Americans in an unprepared manner, in a manner which puts at stake the Government's entire credibility, will do an enormous disservice to Canada. Indeed, this is not a free trade agreement, it is another annexation manifesto.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to make a few comments on Bill C-87, a Bill that is largely a technical one aimed at harmonizing the customs classification system which is due to take effect on January 1 of next year. While this is largely a technical Bill, we want to use this opportunity to speak about the agreement that was reached by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Government with the Reagan administration. We believe that this agreement will have wide-spread adverse consequences for the people of Canada and the future of Canada as a nation.
I have just been looking at the classic work of George Grant, Lament for a Nation, which looks at the fall of the Diefen-baker Government in 1963. While Grant has some sympathy with Diefenbaker and sees him as a person who had a vision of Canada, he felt that Diefenbaker was incapable of really carrying that vision out, that he was incapable of governing in any way that was commensurate with his vision of Canada as an independent country, a country that could be in control of its own destiny. He felt that in many ways, the country had
already been sold down the river by the continentalist approach of C. D. Howe. Of course, today, the natural inheritors of C. D. Howe's vision are sitting once again on the government benches. The Conservative Party has taken over the function of moving Canada into a continentalist economy.
The agreement that was reached in the early days of this past month can be criticized on two grounds. First, its process can be criticized. The process the Government used to reach this agreement was flawed and dishonest from the beginning. We have already quoted extensively from the comments that were made by several of the candidates for the leadership of the Conservative Party in 1983, but I think it is important to drive this message home to the Canadian people, to remind them that when these people were running for the leadership of the Conservative Party and campaigning during the 1984 election campaign, they did not say they were looking to negotiate a free trade deal with the United States. In fact the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark)-

speechtext: Order, please. We are debating Bill C-87. I think it is starting to turn into some sort of a free trade package here, but I would like the Hon. Member to get back to the Bill if at all possible.

Mr. Speaker, certainly I can appreciate that admonition. The Bill which provides for what is known as the harmonized system, the new customs classifications, will allow for the quicker release of goods crossing the border into Canada, and that is a part of what we are talking about.
Even without entering into an agreement, we already have, to a very large extent, free trade with the United States. This Bill will allow for common coding of tariffs and it will encourage freer trade throughout the world. We are talking about the fact that this Government is not content simply to lower tariffs, it is not content simply to liberalize trade, but rather it is basically selling out the future of Canada. This is what I was trying to establish when I was referring to this article from Maclean's of June 15, 1983, in which the present Secretary of State for External Affairs said:
Unrestrained free trade with the United States raises the possibility that thousands of jobs could be lost in such critical industries as textiles, furniture and footwear. Before we jump on the bandwagon of continentalism, we should strengthen our industrial structure so that we are more competitive.
We have not seen that strengthening of the industrial structure. Instead, we have seen the Government dismantling the programs that could have led to a strengthening of that structure.
The Secretary of State, then a candidate for the leadership of the Conservative Party, talked about thousands of jobs which might be lost. The Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard), when he was asked about this a few days ago in the House, said that perhaps 500,000 jobs could be lost, perhaps more, perhaps less. What the Secretary of State said four years ago is still true, yet we are moving toward this free trade agreement with the United States.
