The Secretary of State himself said:
It's silly. Canada must improve relations and trade with the United States, of course. But our natural destiny is to become a global leader, not America's weak sister.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said:
Bilateral free trade with the United States is simplistic and naive. It would only serve to further diminish our ability to compete internationally.
We can only agree with him. The present Prime Minister, then seeking the leadership of the Conservative Party, said in 1983:
Canadians rejected free trade with the United States in 1911. They would do so again in 1983. Canada must increase its share of total world trade, which has dropped by 33 per cent in the past two decades.
If Canada would reject that kind of agreement in 1983, as the Prime Minister said it would, I believe Canada would also reject it in 1987 or 1988 if Canadians get an opportunity to go to the polls on this particular issue.
The point I want to make is that when members of the present Government were running for the leadership of the Conservative Party in 1983, they were very explicit. With the exception of the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), they did not see free trade as a desirable option for Canada to pursue.
When they were engaged in the 1984 election campaign and had a platform to lay before the people of Canada, the vision that they had of Canada, the candidates did not mention free trade as being part of that vision. They did not mention that they would have an agreement with the United States that would give the United States equal access to our energy, an agreement that would gut the possibility of Canada taking action that would allow us to protect our own culture. They did not mention this to the Canadian people so they do not have any real mandate for it.
As soon as the Government was elected in 1984, we began to hear the Prime Minister talking about how the United States is our best friend, and we have to stand up for our best friend, and when our best friend wants something, we should do what we can to accommodate our best friend. Certainly we have been accommodating to our best friends in the United States for the last three years. We have seen one example after another of how this Government has backed down on every demand the United States has made.
The Government backed down and eliminated the National Energy Program. It gutted FIRA. It allowed American takeovers of our book publishing industry after saying it would not. It did not stand up to maintain Canadian ownership of Dome Petroleum. The very week that the free trade negotiations began, the Americans imposed a 35 per cent duty on our shakes and shingles. We saw a 15 per cent tariff applied to our softwood lumber exports. That was later changed because of our weak approach. We said, "Do not apply the tariff, we will apply a tax ourselves", and we added a 15 per cent tax on

softwood. The Americans applied an 85 per cent countervailing duty on our potash. The Government took a completely weak-kneed approach to opposing the Americans in all these cases.

We were assured that the Auto Pact was not on the table. We were assured that culture was not on the table. We were assured that-

The whole process of the talks was characterized by the last-minute aspect when, just before the final deadline, the Minister sat down over some fried chicken and managed to get a deal. What way is that to reach an agreement that is going to affect the future of Canada for the foreseeable future? We are talking about the future of our

children and grandchildren, and the Government has sold out that future in a process which ignores the real wishes of the Canadian people.
In addition to the process by which the initial agreement was reached and signed, we see the process the Government put in place for dealing with that agreement in the House of Commons. Instead of having all the documents available for the committee to study, allowing adequate time for that study and to hear from those who are most affected, so that the committee can reach a reasoned conclusion about whether or not the agreement is good or bad for the Canadian people, it was given a deadline. It has to report to Parliament by December 4, yet it will not have the final text of the agreement until the end of this month. We expect that committee to reach some kind of reasoned, logical conclusion about this agreement, but it will only have the text for a few days. That is a complete betrayal of any concept of parliamentary democracy, and on an issue as important as this. I simply want to emphasize that a bad process cannot lead to a good deal.
The Americans are going to get equal access to our energy resources. We say the agreement gives Canadian culture some protection, but it also says that no Canadian action can infringe on American economic interests in that area. The agreement gives American multinational corporations the power to come in and take over any Canadian company with an asset value of up to $150 million. The threshold used to be $5 million. Only some 500 Canadian companies will have any protection at all if this agreement is ratified.
In conclusion, while this particular Bill might have some value, the free trade agreement goes far beyond what this Bill talks about. We feel that the Canadian people should have a chance to speak on that free trade agreement, and that is why we have been urging the Government to be honest with the Canadian people, tell them they are going to have that chance, and that there will be an election on this issue in the very near future.

Mr. Speaker, I want to respond to the words offered by the Hon. Member in connection with free trade, although not necessarily with the Bill being debated. He asserted that the Government has no mandate to have negotiated the free trade agreement and to have signed it in principle. He asserted that this Parliament has no mandate to deal with the issue, and that raises certain questions which I will put this way.
We did not, in the 1984 election campaign, talk about the specifics of the Meech Lake Accord. We had no way of doing that. What we did was to pledge ourselves to reconciling the nation. The Meech Lake Accord is a way of doing that. That was supported by the NDP without any election campaign commitment or approval. Because Members on both sides, given the experience we have had and the contents of the
agreement, believed that it was good for Canada and it was a valid way of fulfilling that commitment to reconciliation, it was passed in principle just one week ago.
In the 1984 election the Progressive Conservative Party committed itself to renewing the economic strength of the nation. The free trade agreement is one way of doing it. It is a way that has credibility, because through the economic policies of the Government well over 900,000 new jobs have been generated. No one is quarreling with that result.
I suggest that if we quarrel with the free trade agreement it should not be because it was not specifically suggested in the 1984 election campaign but because of particulars which members of the Opposition challenge. I recognize the validity of that. However, if it is not valid for the Government and this Parliament to endorse or defeat that free trade agreement, then I suggest that we had no right to endorse the Meech Lake Accord because it was not specifically in the 1984 campaign either.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member raises a very interesting point. I would like to consider it briefly. First, I think it is important for the Hon. Member to remember what I said at the beginning of my speech, that being that several members of the present Government, including the Minister of Finance, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie), and the Prime Minister, when campaigning to be the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party in 1983 were very explicit in rejecting the concept of a comprehensive free trade agreement with the United States. The present Minister of Transport said that such an agreement was desirable and advocated it. The others, in a public debate, indicated their opposition. They were very clear and forthright about it.
The Canadian people had a pretty clear idea where the Government should have stood on that issue. There was absolutely no indication during the 1984 campaign that the Prime Minister had decided to change his mind on that issue. He changes his mind on a lot of issues, but he did not signal his intention to change his mind on that one.
With regard to the Meech Lake agreement, I think the fact that the ten provinces and the three political Parties which are represented in this House are all basically in agreement with the principle of Meech Lake indicates that there is a drastically different situation in that. In conclusion, while Meech Lake is not going to destroy Canada as a nation, there is as very strong feeling among a lot of people across Canada, and certainly within this Party, that the free trade agreement which the Prime Minister has reached with the United States will destroy Canada and that the vision of Canada which we have had for over 120 years is going down the tube because of this agreement.
Due to that, I think it is very important for the Hon. Member to think back to the commitment which he made to
November 2, 1987

his constituents in 1984 and to ask himself whether the agreement which is being negotiated right now with the United States, which gives equal access to our energy to the United States, under which we do not have the capacity to protect our culture, under which American companies can come across the border and take over any company worth up to $150 million, and under which we can impose no content or performance requirements for those takeovers, is in keeping with the commitment he made to his constituents in 1984 and whether he wants to fight an election on that issue. If he does not want to fight an election on that issue, why not?

Mr. Speaker, subsequent to the 1984 election the Government initiated the appointment of a joint committee of the House and the Senate to study Canada's international relations, its initial responsibility being, among other things, the study of a free trade proposal. The Government did not enter into free trade negotiations on the basis of a whim or change of mind within the Cabinet. It did so after the special joint committee, representing both Chambers of Parliament, went from one coast to the other and heard substantial testimony from all manner of citizens and was persuaded to recommend to the Government that it enter into negotiations for a free trade agreement.
The same recommendation was made by the Macdonald Royal Commission on Canada's economic future. Both the parliamentary committee and the royal commission reached the conclusion that such a free trade agreement offered the greatest promise for Canada's economic future.
I made a commitment to the people of Scarborough West in 1984, that we would renew the economy, that through the stimulation of the private sector we would produce jobs, jobs, jobs. Since 1984 that is precisely what the Government has done, that is precisely what the country has enjoyed. No election commitment has been more honorably and fully met in the history of the country.

Mr. Speaker, when the joint committee travelled across Canada it heard substantial testimony from organizations representing hundreds of thousands of Canadians who opposed the concept of a free trade agreement with the United States. Our Party certainly did not agree with the final report which spoke of a free trade agreement with the United States. There was no consensus arrived at by that special joint committee.
With regard to jobs, in my riding the rate of unemployment is still unacceptably high. If the Hon. Member wants to have an election on the issue of jobs after looking at the rates of unemployment in British Columbia, New Brunswick and Newfoundland, let the Government call an election, then we can find out whether the people are satisfied with the record of the Government on that issue. I say that in my area they are not.

Mr. Speaker, the temptation to leap into the fray is strong. I would like my colleague to comment on the
Mint and Currency
relevance of the debate today. Customs tariffs, which we are debating today, are an absolutely critical part of an industrial strategy. Trade agreements are absolutely critical to such a strategy, and trade strategy is shaped through customs tariffs.
Although this Bill is passed off by the Government as a very small, technical piece of legislation, I believe that customs tariffs have far-reaching effects on trade agreements and industrial strategies in the country. I know that you recognize that, Mr. Speaker, and that is why we have been allowed to speak on a more wide-ranging subject. Some of the more narrow-minded Conservatives in this place may fail to see the relevance of that. Perhaps my colleague could comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps the best example of the relevance of the Customs Tariff is the fact that the free trade agreement which the Government just finished negotiating removes the tariff on the Auto Pact which has not been used for a number of years. That was the one club which the Canadian industry had to ensure that the Americans honoured the details of the Auto Pact. By removing the tariff we have given away the farm with regard to the Auto Pact. We no longer have any effective enforcement mechanism to back up the Auto Pact. The issue of tariffs with which we are dealing in Bill C-87 is very important to the question of an industrial strategy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at length on this Bill, but I wonder if the Government might give us a few notes or a few explanations on the scope of this very important legislation which is being amended by Bill C-77 so that we may have a democratic debate on this whole question, namely that the Bill is "to authorize the taking of special temporary measures to ensure safety and security during national emergencies and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof'. As I just said, Mr. Speaker, I do not have any notes on this question, but I vividly remember the October crisis and the severe criticisms which were made at the time about some of
the provisions. I should think that this parliamentary initiative, this Bill C-77, is aimed at making some amendments to the legislation and making it more acceptable to Canadians. Therefore, I would have thought the Government would have provided explanations, without going too far, without encouraging them too much, to the Hon. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There are no questions or comments. The Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) has the floor on debate.

Mr. Speaker, I had no idea that we would get to Bill C-77 so quickly today. It was my understanding that it would be called tomorrow or later in the week, and that we would be discussing Bill C-76. I understand it has passed second reading stage.
I sincerely hope that Bill C-76 will go to committee because it requires very serious scrutiny.
Bill C-76 has been sent to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I have much to say about Bill C-77. As my Party's defence spokesperson, I want to put on the record the very serious misgivings we have with respect to this new legislation that will replace the War Measures Act.
Therefore, I welcome the opportunity to lead this debate on behalf of the New Democratic Party. Let me say at the outset that New Democrats are determined that the War Measures Act should never be used again. That is why we are happy that the Minister has brought forward a proposal to replace the War Measures Act. It has been a long time in coming and I congratulate him for finally bringing this debate to the floor of the House of Commons.
His Bill is a good first try, in my judgment, although it is not perfect by any means.
I will use this opportunity to explain in detail my very deep concerns relating to Bill C-77.
First, I want to say that I hope the parliamentary process, particularly in committee, will be allowed to work. We have heard many nice words from the Government about the spirit of parliamentary reform. In truth, we have made some progress thanks to the work of the committee led by the former Member for St. John's East and now the Lieutenant Governor of Newfoundland.
Now it is time for the parliamentary process to shine. We will need many hearings and a great deal of testimony from both expert witnesses and ordinary Canadians. This is an issue which touches the very lives and liberties of every Canadian. It involves an issue that cuts to the very heart of the Canadian consciousness. Is there anyone in this House who was not in some way touched by the events of October, 1970? Who could not be affected by the profoundly un-Canadian sight of Canadian troops in battle dress in the streets to suppress the domestic troubles of their fellow citizens?
Emergencies-Act
I do not want to reopen old wounds. Instead, I hope that this Bill as amended will complete the healing process. Together with the evolution of our Canadian Constitution I hope that the replacement of the War Measures Act will close one chapter in our history and usher in a new era in which the rights and freedoms of all Canadians will be honoured and respected at all times and in all circumstances.
The roots of the War Measures Act are deep. They go back much further than 1970. The original Act was born in August of 1914 when the First World War broke out. The Government of the day found that it had virtually no laws to deal with the situation. So it rushed through this law. It was modelled on foreign legislation. It received almost no debate. It had virtually no consideration. In effect, it gave the Government a blank cheque. Parliament and the people of Canada surrendered all their rights at that time in 1914.
The War Measures Act allowed censorship, arbitrary arrest, travel restrictions and Government control of trade and property. There were no rights untouched. In effect, it provided for an authoritarian Government to replace a democratic Government without a shot being fired. I suppose that we should not be surprised by the problems this caused later on. It was a recipe for disaster. The process was so poor there was little thought that a bad law was perhaps unavoidable.
Let us not repeat this fatal error again. We need full debate. We must hear many points of view. We should deliberate in an air of calm and reason. There is no emergency at this time. We have time to consider what we are setting in place for future generations. There is no war. There is no apprehended insurrection, no violence, no upheaval. Now is the time to give it straightforward, serious, cautious and deliberate consideration.
It is the future that we must be concerned about. For if the War Measures Act shows us one thing" it is that people suffer for past mistakes. Following the Russian revolution suspected dissidents were interned in Canada because of the extraordinary powers in the War Measures Act. The Communist Party was outlawed. Even Jehova's Witnesses were suspect. The political and religious freedoms that we are bound to uphold in this place were denied by Canadians. One of the most bitter of all ironies is that in the fight against communism we outlawed a communist party here in Canada which is precisely the same kind of authoritarian action that a communist Government would take. Therefore in doing so we reduced, or diminished to a considerable extent, the dynamism of our own democracy.
Again, in the Second World War thousands of Canadians of Japanese origin were interned. Racism raised its ugly head. The bitter legacy of this tragic episode still haunts the Canadian Government today. Japanese Canadians are still waiting for redress and for justice.
As I have already mentioned, many were arrested without warrant and held without bail in the October crisis of 1970. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) will

November 2, 1987
Emergencies-Act
remember that well. I believe he was Minister of Justice at the time. Many other Members will also recall that sorry episode.
Again, I do not wish to appear as if I were looking back with the wisdom of hindsight, but it is always a tragedy of inestimable proportions when a legislative body such as this, the supreme legislative body of the land, deliberately and knowingly passes legislation that it knows will deny basic human rights and freedoms to the citizens of a democracy, one of the great democracies in the world today, our own country.
1 know that New Democrats remember that period very well. We have our own reasons. The public approved of the measure and Parliament favoured the proclamation by a vote of 190 to 16. The 16 were ridiculed, but they stood firm and history has vindicated them. That is one reason why the memory of Tommy Douglas is held in such high esteem in this country.
Later, of course, successive Liberal Governments recognized their error and tried to reform the War Measures Act. But nothing ever came before this House. That is why it is galling to listen to Liberal Members criticize this Bill, as no doubt they will and have. They were in government for 14 years after 1970 and did nothing to correct this problem.
One effort to at least examine the problem came from the task force on Canadian unity. It recommended that the Government have the right to seek parliamentary approval within a specified time limit for any extraordinary powers. It also recommended that the Government state the reasons for its actions and the duration of the emergency powers in its proclamation. The task force further recommended that provincial powers and individual rights be safeguarded to various degrees depending on whether the nation was at war or at peace. I am happy to see the bones of some of those recommendations in the Minister's proposals. We will try in the legislative process to improve upon them.
We will have help, of course. I do not pretend to have all the answers in this debate at second reading. I do not think anyone in this Chamber has. I hope that experts from such groups as the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association and others will give us their professional suggestions. Perhaps some of those Canadians who suffered from the excesses of the War Measures Act should come before our committee. I want to know whether they would feel any safer with this proposed law on the law books. If this Bill would not prevent such disastrous mistakes from happening again, then in our judgment it is useless.
We shall also look forward to hearing from the Minister in committee. It will be interesting to know what thinking went into this Bill. For instance, the McDonald Commission did not think that the Government needed any additional emergency powers in peacetime.
What has changed since the McDonald Royal Commission report was published? We have had disasters such as the Mississauga train derailment that required mass evacuation,
but that was carried out without resorting to the War Measures Act. Why does the Government need such powers now? This is something else that we should look at in committee. I am not suggesting that the Government should not have these powers, but I think that the onus resides with the Minister and his experts to prove to this House that he needs these extraordinary powers in order to deal with that kind of an emergency.
I have other specific concerns about this Bill as well. I would like to put some of them on the record this afternoon. Under the section dealing with public welfare emergencies the Bill speaks of an emergency as a "breakdown in the flow of essential goods, services or resources". That would seem to have very serious implications for the right to strike.
A recent Supreme Court decision said that the right to strike is not protected by the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. So the Minister's assurances about this Bill being subject to the Charter is of no comfort to working people who may from time to time find themselves involved in a strike situation.
Another recent example shows that this power may not be necessary. That is the recent rail strike. It was an unfortunate incident, but it illustrates the point that I am making. During that strike the Government brought forward legislation that returned the rail workers to their jobs. The Government was not prevented from acting quickly. It did not use the War Measures Act. Why then does it seek new, special powers in peacetime? This is a very touchy subject.
Those who belong to trade unions whose activities span the nation such as in transportation, whether it is air, rail, or shipping, those who are involved in communications, and those who are involved in the postal services, whether it is inside or outside workers, all of those persons could feel that their rights are being infringed upon, or potentially infringed upon, if this Bill is passed without any change.
In response to the Government's back to work legislation, there were protests on Parliament Hill and elsewhere. Peaceful protest is the right of those affected. They had a right to register their displeasure. Under this Bill such a protest could have been prevented. I ask again, does the Government need such power? Should it have such power? These questions must be thoroughly discussed, debated, and reflected upon when this Bill goes to committee.
Probably the most contentious clause of this Bill is the one that deals with public order emergencies. This is the type of situation that gave rise to the use of the War Measures Act in 1970. This clause takes its definition of threat from the Canadian Security and Intelligence Service Act. This fact alone should make us very cautious, because of the difficulties already encountered with CSIS, in determining what is subversion and what is legitimate dissent.
This has always been a very difficult issue to resolve in this Chamber, and indeed in other democratic bodies throughout
November 2, 1987

the world. In my view, one of the things that keeps a democracy healthy is the right of its citizens to dissent, to object, and to oppose. It is often of a very negative nature, but nonetheless it is the right of a citizen to stand up in public and disagree with the Government, disagree with a law, suggest that the law is changed, or state that the regulation is a bad one.
It is a far different situation if someone is actively engaged in planning or executing a subversive action. That is something quite different. Most intelligence gathering agencies and most counter-intelligence gathering agencies, whether it is the FBI in the United States, MI-5 in Britain, or CSIS in Canada, find it extremely difficult to delineate the difference between legitimate dissent in a democracy, which should be welcomed, and subversive activity, which is clearly illegal.
The CSIS Act cites activities "in support of the threat or use of acts of serious violence against persons or property for the purpose of achieving a political objective within Canada or a foreign state".
I would remind the Minister that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) recently met with Oliver Tambo of the African National Congress. The ANC has not renounced violence in its fight against apartheid. I hope that the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State did not promise to support the ANC. Otherwise they might have to have themselves arrested under this Bill, if it becomes an Act of Parliament. That may sound rather ridiculous and extreme. Nonetheless, if one studies the wording of the CSIS interpretation of subversion, it is found that it is a pretty wide open interpretation and could include or involve all types of legitimate legal activity. It may rub the Government of the day the wrong way, whether it is Conservative, Liberal, or NDP, but nonetheless Governments in a democracy do have to tolerate legitimate dissent.
Others on the government benches have had contact with the Reagan administration, which supports the effort of the Contras in Nicaragua. The Contras use violence, and President Reagan spoke of their cause in this very Chamber. Should that be illegal in Canada? I am quite sure that most of my colleagues across the way would disagree and say that that is perfectly legal, and I agree that it is perfectly legal. Again, if a narrow interpretation is attached to the CSIS interpretation of what is a subversion then, of course, Bill C-77 becomes potentially dangerous.
A public order emergency also gives Cabinet the right to prohibit public assembly. But how could a Canadian avail himself of the right to protest peacefully the declaration of emergency powers? His right to disagree with government policy would be extremely limited.
Similarly, a legitimate protest against the emergency declaration could be suppressed and no one would find out. The Government could censor the media or simply forbid travel to the troubled area. How could anyone find out if the declaration of an emergency was justified if no one was allowed in or out of the area? How could parliamentarians
Emergencies-Act
rally public support against an unjust proclamation if the public was being kept in the dark? That is all included in this Bill as presently written. In committee we will chop through those clauses, clean them up, and make the definition much clearer and more limited.
I also have concerns about the clause dealing with international emergencies. The definition of an international emergency is extremely broad. The Bill speaks of a threat to "any country in which the political, economic or security interests of Canada or any of its allies are involved". That pretty well covers the global waterfront.
Our allies include the United States and western Europe which have very extensive trade interests around the world. In fact, it is hard to think of any country on earth where either Canada, the United States, or western Europe does not have some type of political or economic interest.
We have a perfect example right now in the Persian Gulf. The United States is escorting tankers through one of the most militarily dangerous stretches of water in the world. Other European nations are also involved because they have an economic interest in oil from that region. What would happen if another "Stark" incident blew up into a major confrontation? Canada could become involved under the terms of this legislation. There would probably be a great debate as to whether Canada's vital interests were involved. But the Government would have the right to mobilize first and answer questions later. I would not want to wake up one morning and read that the Government had declared an international emergency and have to wait for the matter to come before Parliament after the fact.
One of the reasons that I would not be comfortable in that situation is the other extraordinary powers that the Government could assume during a perceived international emergency. For example, Cabinet could authorize search and seizure without reference to the courts. Why does it need to bypass the justice system? Are the courts not to be trusted in an emergency? Have judges in this country ever shown themselves to be less than vigilant in their devotion to national security? It is their job to balance the interests and rights of the state and those of the individual. Yet the Government wants the right to enter any home without reference to the courts at any level. Clearly this part of the Bill is unacceptable to those of us in the New Democratic Party.
Finally, Parliament must consider the total discretion granted to Cabinet under the terms of a war emergency. It is difficult to see any difference between this clause and the current War Measures Act. I wonder why some powers could not be set out in the Bill. Canada has been in two world wars. Does the Government not have any idea what powers it needs to mobilize the Armed Forces? Could they not be added to the powers listed in the other clauses of the Bill?
I see that my time today has run out, Mr. Speaker. I look forward to continuing debate at a later time.

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, October 1st, consideration of the motion of Mr. Nickerson that Bill C-211, an Act to amend the FreshWater Fish Marketing Act, be read a second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to address the House, at the beginning of this second hour, on the motion moved by the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson).
In order to understand what we are trying to do here, I think it must be said that the purpose of the Bill which is going to be debated is to remove the monopoly presently enjoyed by the FreshWater Fish Marketing Board for interprovincial and international marketing of fish and fish products.
To remind you of the mandate given to that Board, it was established in 1969, under the FreshWater Fish Marketing Act, for the purpose of marketing fish and fish products. The
Board has a monopoly over marketing and trading in fish on interprovincial and export markets. It exercises this monopoly itself or through its agents, first to ensure an orderly marketing and, second, to increase fishermen's income, and third, find international markets for our fish and increase interprovincial trade and fish exports.
The participation of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Ontario and the Northwest Territories was established in agreement with the Government of Canada. The FFMC is a Crown Corporation covered by Schedule C, Part I, of the Financial Administration Act. It must carry out its operations independently without appropriations from Parliament.
The major purpose of the Corporation is to provide the highest possible income to commercial fishermen based on their catches, and all its activities contribute to this end. The Corporation keeps informed of the social effects of its interventions, but will not support the cost elements which can be directly attributed to the taking into account of these social considerations.
If a provincial or federal department or agency decides to apply social considerations to the activities of the Corporation to meet objectives other than the provision of the highest possible income for fishermen, such a department or agency will have to support the costs related to this intervention.
Mr. Speaker, both in agriculture and in other sectors of our economy, especially the agro-food sector, there is an increasing demand for marketing boards, particularly from farmers and producers. Yet, this Bill aims at abolishing a marketing board which, in 1986-87, had one of the most successful of its eighteen years according to its own report and to the comments of its Chairman. Its sales have totalled nearly $59 million, $10 million more than the record amount registered the previous year. Net revenues before final payments amounted to $14 million, $6 million more than the record set two years ago.
One very important fact is that the disposable income of fishermen has reached $36.6 million, $7 million more than the last record high.
Mr. Speaker, I think the Corporation, at least as far as 1986-87 is concerned, has indeed met our expectations, which were to find new markets for fish and find the best possible price for our fishermen so they can earn a decent living.
According to the president's report, and I quote:
Strong demand for fish and seafood products in Canada and the United States assisted us in reaching many objectives for our major species.
For species such as Pickerel, Sauger and Northern Pike whose landings were in balance with market demands, selling prices were excellent. For species whose supply had previously exceeded demand such as Lake Trout progress was made in eliminating or reducing inventory. We had a record sales volume for Whitefish, but an increase in landings prevented inventory reduction. However, we are optimistic the chronic over-supply of Whitefish will be alleviated in 1987/88.
We continue to improve in all aspects of our operations and believe the Corporation is properly positioned with the products and the people to
November 2, 1987

participate fully in the ongoing growth of the fish and seafood industry for the benefit of our 3,500 fishermen.
Mr. Speaker, in my view the Corporation plays a vital role in providing 3,500 fishermen with a decent income. I am convinced if we were to get rid of the Corporation prematurely, without consultation with the provinces-because what the Hon. Member is proposing is to abolish the Corporation unilaterally.
As I said earlier, the Corporation was created jointly with and with the agreement of the provinces-
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are indicating to me that my time is almost over and that I may not be able to complete my remarks. My point is that fish producers are the ones who directly depend on the Corporation to earn an adequate income in order to support their families and not have to resort to unemployment insurance or welfare to make a decent living in this country.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that to abolish this marketing board would be contrary to the will of the producers, in agriculture or elsewhere. Farmers are exerting considerable pressures for the creation of more marketing boards. We are presently considering a request from potato producers.
Why do the producers wish to have these boards? It is simply because they want to get a fair retribution for their work, they want a decent living for their families, they do not want to live all their lives on public charity.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is premature to abolish the Corporation at this time. It would run contrary to the will of our government which is trying to find the best ways to provide adquate incomes to all Canadians.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would simply express the hope that this marketing board will not disappear as quickly as the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) would like.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. speaker, I welcome the opportunity to comment briefly on the Bill presently before us. At this time I want to say that I am neither for nor against Bill C-211. However, I have some serious concerns about fishermen who are served by the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. Will it serve their interest to have this marketing agency disbanded? I believe we have to ask ourselves why the corporation was brought into being in the first place. The answer is quite simple. In the early 1960s the inland fishery and fish trade were in serious difficulty. They were experiencing difficulties similar to those which afflicted the salt fish industry in Atlantic Canada. Consequently a federal-provincial conference was held in October 1964 in Ottawa to identify the problem areas relating to the inland fishery. As a result of this conference a commission of inquiry into the freshwater fish marketing was established in 1965. The terms of reference for Commissioner G. Mclvor included instructions to inquire into the underlying factors which contributed to the weaknesses in the export
Freshwater Fish Marketing Act
prices of freshwater fish. The commission completed its findings and prepared its recommendations in 1966.
The commission reported that prices for round or dressed fish in export markets were weak because there were too many exporters to counter a control exercise by a few importers. It also reported that in marketing of round or dressed fish, Canadian exporters were receiving too small a share of the prices paid by consumers. The commission recommended that a fresh fish marketing board be established under federal jurisdiction; that the board be the sole seller of freshwater fish produced in the designated areas; and that the board pool the returns from the sale of fish and fish products.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), when he was speaking in this debate on October 1 said that the single desk selling system did not really work out, that the commercial clout that was supposed to have been given to the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation never really materialized in fact and things had gone from bad to worse. During its first year of operation when it was established in 1969 I believe, the FFMC generated sales of $14.4 million. It is interesting to note that since then each year sales have increased. In 1986-87 sales generated $58.6 million. It is also interesting to note that currently approximately 70 per cent of the wholesale price for fish marketed by the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation is returned to the fishermen.
Although I am sure my colleague from the Western Arctic has the greatest concern in the entrepreneurial spirit for private companies to be involved and not a government agency to be the sole marketer of fish, I am concerned that if prices should drop in the market-place for freshwater fish that, occurred in the early 1960s might happen to this industry. I share the same concerns for the disbandment of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation as I would express if there were an attempt to disband the Canadian Saltfish Corporation. I believe they were not set up by Government just for the mere fact of having a government agency in place. They were set up to serve the fishermen and the industry as a whole with the greatest of intent to improve conditions.
I am neither for nor against the Bill at this time, but I still want to caution Members present that the Bill deserves a very serious look and we should give it our very serious attention. We should not act in a hasty manner and create great havoc in an industry which is doing quite well at the present time.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Bill before the House is in the name of the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson). He has introduced it, I suppose, for the past eight, nine or ten years, as I recall, to try to get rid of the monopoly in the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. In his particular area and down through western Canada there is one marketing agency, one corporation, set up by the federal Government to buy all of that freshwater fish and then sell it. It is a complete monopoly. If a private

November 2, 1987
Freshwater Fish Marketing Act
businessman wishes to buy some freshwater white fish-a very popular fish-and he figures he has a market in the United States or Europe for that fish, he can pay more for the white fish than the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation can pay to the fishermen. He is able to pay more and he can get more for that white fish, if it is good white fish, in the United States or in Europe. But according to the law, he is not allowed to do that because the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation has the sole right to buy and market that fish.
We have the same situation on the East Coast of Canada with salt fish. A businessman can come along and say, "I can pay you more for your fish because it is of excellent quality". Perhaps he can pick a part of the coastline where the fishermen catch the biggest fish and bleed the fish properly so that it is of better quality than the general amount of fish being exported. Perhaps the individual can get more in the marketplace, but he is not allowed because the law says that there is only one marketing agent for salt fish in Canada and that is the Canadian Saltfish Corporation.
Many businessmen came to the Progressive Conservatives when they were running in the last election. They asked them, "If you get in power, for goodness' sake change the law so that private business people can buy and sell salt fish and freshwater fish". The Progressive Conservative Party met with these business people and said yes. In fact, the Progressive Conservative Party said, "Yes, we will free you from the monopolistic practices of the previous Government because we will boot it out. They are the ones who set up these corporations that control and monopolize the market-place. These corporations are the only ones allowed to buy, sell and market all of these products in Canada.
In fact, the Progressive Conservative campaign handbook says the following on page 47:
We will reduce the role of crown corporations in the fishery as we create
economic conditions that allow private companies and fishermen's co-ops to
prosper.
Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative Party, and nobody can blame it for doing this, met with these business people on the East Coast and in central Canada, who wanted to get into the business of buying and selling fish, salt fish and freshwater fish. That is what it came up with as a policy.
What has the Progressive Conservative Government done? Since it has been in power, the only thing the Progressive Conservative Government has done with the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation that I can see is that it appointed a prominent Progressive Conservative to be the Chairman of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. That is all that was done, to my recollection.
Instead of changing the corporation, the Government appointed a chairman. Mind you, this particular Chairman is a chartered accountant, the author of two books on taxation, a prominent gentleman who used to write, as I recall, very good
columns in the Winnipeg Free Press once upon a time. That is all the Progressive Conservative Party did with the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation.
Now we have this Bill before us today. As far as the positions of the political Parties are concerned, I can now say that the Progressive Conservative Party stands fully behind the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. So does the New Democratic Party and so does the Liberal Party. This is because they have taken the position that the general good of all the fishermen in those areas should be the primary concern of the Government. In other words, there should be one marketing agent that would be able to perform in the way a cartel performs by regulating prices in the market-place. The political Parties have said furthermore that in this way, the Government of Canada can very easily assist the industry at times when prices go down and fluctuate in the market-place.
One can understand the position taken by the hon. gentleman who introduced the Bill. Perhaps some of the best freshwater fish is in his area. Perhaps up in the Arctic in his particular area, there are business people who are telling the fishermen that they can market the fish for a better price. Maybe he represents that kind of an area. Perhaps that fish is put in with other fish from other areas of Canada that is not as good as the fish from his area.
All of us who represent fisheries areas know what the Hon. Member is talking about. For example, on the northeast coast of Newfoundland, there is better salt fish than in other parts of eastern Canada, but our fish goes in with the salt fish from other areas to be marketed by the Canadian Saltfish Corporation.
As I say, the official position of the three political Parties of the House of Commons is in favour of this marketing structure, this Crown corporation. The hon. gentleman will just have to accept defeat and realize that he will not get such a Bill through the House of Commons.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this Bill, I think it would be prudent first to ask the House to recognize the prosperity and positive market conditions which Canada's freshwater fishing industry has recently enjoyed. Fresh fish are a wholesome and healthy product whose consumer acceptance in our major market in the United States appears to be growing. As with all good things, I hope this surge of prosperity continues.
Yet this is not a time for complacency. I refer specifically to the interim report on freshwater fisheries of the Senate Standing Committee on Fisheries tabled in September of 1986 entitled The Marketing of Fish in Canada. I recommend this excellent report to anyone who wishes a general overview of the freshwater fisheries, their markets, their problems, their concerns and their opportunities.
The report deals with these issues and especially the concept of a single-desk system of marketing as now used by the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation for Canada's
November 2, 1987

freshwater fisheries. The report gives a glimpse of the future of our fisheries, the opportunities as well as the pitfalls.
I will refer to these matters in some detail, but going directly to the point, the report refers to activities of the FFMC and consistently indicates that provincial co-operation, which I remind the House was instrumental in the establishment of the corporation, be sought and encouraged. It is abundantly clear that co-operation with the provinces is crucial to the success of the freshwater fisheries of the western region covered by the corporation.
Today, the provinces and the vast majority of the fishermen continue to support the FFMC and the findings of the report are also pertinent in this manner. These findings, the result of 25 hearings, 17 of which were devoted exclusively to the freshwater fisheries, and 40 submissions could not have had a clearer thrust in the substance of their recommendations. These recommendations address a wide range of issues and challenges facing the fishery including new technology, overparticipation, over-capitalization at the processing level, insufficient development of local markets, product substitution, and the introduction of potentially crippling import duties by our major market, the United States.
With respect to the challenges of making products available on a year-round basis, of co-ordination of supply and especially of the management of large inventories and delivery surges, the committee stated that the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation devotes considerable resources to unload these inventories, continually seeking out and developing new markets. As a central marketing organization set up to accomplish precisely this task, the corporation has on balance a good record of success. It is a record to which my colleagues have referred today and it has proven to be even more successful within the last year.
Let us examine some of these problems and challenges that are being faced by the freshwater fishermen of our western region and the contribution of the corporation in facing these challenges in more detail.
Single desk selling, as examined by the report, brings greatest over-all benefit when created to consolidate the efforts of a dispersed production. It can also be useful in industries where production varies widely according to the season. It can also provide for streamlining of the marketing process. Greater control can be exercised over quality and variety of products, speed of delivery, and flexibility in transport and payment terms. The single desk system can mobilize resources to seek out markets.
I suppose the area covered by the corporation, 5.34 million square kilometres with a population of less than five million, qualifies as a dispersed area. Indeed, it is larger than most of the world's nations, perhaps as dispersed as any harvesting area in the world. The 23 species of fish appeal to many different markets.
Freshwater Fish Marketing Act
The U.S. is by far the leading market for the products of the freshwater fishery. The harvest of Canada's freshwater fishery does not, however, figure prominently in the total U.S. supply picture. This is because there is substantial production of freshwater fish in the U.S. As well, other nations have aggressive marketing policies for their products. Fortunately, there is now a healthy trend within the U.S. toward increased per capita consumption of fresh fish. However, consumer behaviour is easily changed by prices. Experts believe that price rises for fish products, mainly the result of higher production costs, may soon lead to product switching and the substitution of cheaper protein.
The American consumer is demanding. That is the reality facing Canadian fishermen. We are not the only ones selling our wares. Reliability of supply, price, quality, and attractive presentation to and education of the buyer are often the difference between success and failure in the supermarket. The committee could not be clearer on how to achieve that success: "The Canadian freshwater fishing industry should also endeavour to make its products available in the market-place on a broad scale and on a year round basis." It is that sort of activity which has been addressed by the FFMC. The expertise has a broader application to our fisheries as well.
Let me take a moment to recount some of the problems our freshwater fishery faces. These problems have been tackled by the corporation in co-operation with the provinces. Cooperation is the key word. They have looked at the question of over-participation, overcapitalization, and insufficient development of local markets. These problems are also opportunities. They present an ideal example of potential for continuing constructive co-operation with the provinces. Provincial initiative has always been an important corner-stone of opportunity for the freshwater fishery. Indeed, the committee realized that, and this brings me to the second theme spoken of by my colleagues, that of the role of the provinces in the success of our fishery.
Over-participation and overcapitalization at the processing level may very well create havoc in the fishery. In 1984 the average harvest of 6,435 kilograms generated average gross revenue of $8,222. This overcapitalization at the processing level raises the cost of bringing a product to market, creates pressure for higher prices, and raises expectations for higher than possible gains. The recommendation by the committee to cope with this problem was that the provincial and territorial Governments, in co-operation with the FFMC, co-ordinate their efforts to bring about a good balance of investment in harvesting facilities among participants in the western fishery, given the harvestable quantity of fish. It is that co-operation which sounds a signal note for the future prosperity of our fishery. Other speakers have referred to provincial initiatives in the establishment of the corporation. What better example might we have of the continuing need for provincial input and support than in the recommendation to eliminate the pressing problem of overcapitalization at the processing level.

November 2, 1987
Freshwater Fish Marketing Act
Provincial participation and co-operation always was and always will be a necessity for the success of the fishery. This applies to similar recommendations with regard to the allocation of fish stocks, product substitution, and development of local markets.
These examples of provincial participation are meant to add to what is a matter of great concern to the provinces. Given the onslaught of new technology, especially in aquaculture, the need for co-ordination of supply, the over-participation and overcapitalization, and insufficient development of local markets, product substitution, and potentially crippling export duties, now is the time to focus all possible co-ordinated efforts to maintain the health of the fishery.
I can foresee potential difficulties for our freshwater fishery if the FFMC is limited in its ability to co-operate with the provinces and face these challenges. We should not forget that the freshwater fishery is as important to many of our small communities as is the fishery to the Atlantic coast communities. These problems are a test of the fortitude and skill of the Canadian fishermen.
Finally, I agree with the thrust and substance of the excellent report produced by the Senate Standing Committee on Fisheries. We know the participating provinces and the vast majority of fishermen support the FFMC. A bright future for the fishery and continued profits for the fishermen can result from continuation of this partnership. Thus we should continue to forge the bonds of the partnership, unique in the history of this growing fishery, between the six Governments which founded the FFMC and which led to success for the fishery and profits for the fishermen.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak today on Bill C-211 sponsored by the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), my neighbour to the north. He has brought to the attention of Members of this House the fact that there could be some discrepancies in this marketing board which may or may not be to the benefit of his constituents, but certainly not to mine. This gives me an opportunity to tell you about the many lakes and rivers in the northern part of my constituency in Saskatchewan. Most of you probably do not know that there are more lakes in Saskatchewan than there are in Manitoba and Alberta combined. Of course, there are a lot of fish in those lakes.
Before the marketing board was set up, there were at least six different places in my constituency where fishermen caught fish. The industry provided employment for a good many people in the North. We supplied an excellent quality fish which could be purchased in my home town, the City of Prince Albert, and many other places to the south.
Today of course it is a different story. We now have no one working in the industry other than the fishermen themselves. They must first haul ice to where the fish are caught, pack the fish in ice and then haul them back again, truck the whole fish down to Winnipeg, having only removed the head and guts,
where they are then processed further. Yet now we cannot buy that product in my home town or in Prince Albert. It is just not available. It all seems to go to the United States. The Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation has not done its job of making that fish available in other places.
The cost has been fantastic. The fishermen are receiving 70 per cent of the payout after freight and deductions. When you are hauling fish from Stony Rapids, Saskatchewan, you have to fly them to Wollaston Lake where you put them on a truck to haul them to Winnipeg. It is obviously the trucker who makes the money rather than the poor fisherman. The price of gas and equipment has gone up far in excess of the increase they have received in the past few years.
I hear everyone talking about the increase in sales. I have a book, should anyone be interested in borrowing it, entitled How to Lie with Statistics. That is exactly what the fish marketing people are doing. They say that in 1969 they sold $14 million worth of fish and in 1987 they sold $58 million worth. There was not a damn pound more sold but the price went up. You can sell the same amount and still raise your sales as long as you get more money for it. I do not buy that one.
It does not sit too well in my craw when 1 listen to people up north talking about getting 10 cents and 12 cents a pound for fish when fishermen on the Great Lakes probably get 40 cents or 50 cents a pound. They certainly have a tremendous advantage over the fishermen in the North. The fish may not be as good, but that is the way it goes.
The last time I was up north the fishermen were trying to develop a better marketing system with the freshwater fish marketing people. As a result of attending the meeting which I did, I could see that the chance of them getting much more for their fish was pretty slim.
There is always a good side to such things as this. In this case it would be tourists fishing for trophy fish. I believe that as long as the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation is handling the fish from my area and that of my neighbour in the North we will have to concentrate on trophy fishing because most fishermen will not take their boats out in the weather with which they have to deal during the seasons that they can catch fish for the paltry sums which they get out of it, and I do not blame them. They have ideas about selling on their own, but it is against the law. They are not even allowed to peddle a little bit to their neighbours.
It appears that the only solution will be trophy fish. All the people who are so in favour of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation should save their money and come on up to catch a big trout or big pike to hang on their mantle. That would be their contribution to solving the problem in the North.

control over markets, supply, and quality, although that is not always the case.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to say a few words on Bill 0211. This has been a genuine financial success story which is rather unique in that it has blended the skill and entrepreneurial initiative of the Canadian freshwater fishermen with legislative co-operation between the federal Government and its governmental counterparts in four provinces and the Northwest Territories. It is a success story which proves

November 2, 1987
Adjournment Debate
that co-operation between provinces and the federal Government can forge profits in the rough and tumble of the marketplace.
The Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation resulted from the focus of the collective will of the Government of Canada, in co-operation with the Provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, and the Northwest Territories to introduce application of what is known as the single desk selling system for freshwater fish.
The results of this system are shown by the recent profitability of the corporation, and dramatically increased returns to fishermen. I want to go further, and to bring facts and hard numbers to a debate that is certainly not new in the Hansard of the House of Commons and on which the Hon. Member who introduced it has spoken many times. I am glad that we are not the first to be concerned with these matters, as they affect the interest of our freshwater fishermen, a group whose recent successes must be placed in the context of future challenges.
Let me first recall that the purpose of this corporation was to solve five major financial and economic problems which had been identified by the Province of Manitoba in a brief presented to the National Fisheries Council held in Ottawa in January, 1964. The problems were ones which hopefully can be consigned to our past.
They included disorderly marketing, too many exporters, poor processing equipment, inadequate quality control facilities, and fishermen receiving too low a share of the prices, prices which were constantly fluctuating. That is certainly not a pretty picture and a far cry from today's prosperous industry. But it was different then.
These problems, as described by the commission of inquiry chaired by Mr. George Mclvor, placed the fishermen in the western inland fishery in an appalling position of weakness. The commission said clearly:
We find that under these circumstances, the fisherman is essentially an
indentured labourer for the fish companies.
Not just the commission, but also four provincial governments and the Northwest Territories believed that Canada and its regions needed a strong presence in the diverse markets for freshwater fish to survive and prosper. That was 1965, and the corporation was established in 1969 by the Freshwater Fish Marketing Act.
While I would like to provide some of the Figures, time will not permit. We have come a long way from the days of the individual producer being an indentured labourer for the fish companies, and the spectre of grinding, unending debt that prompted that description by the Mclvor Commission. Last year, total payments to fishermen increased from $28.1 million to $36.6 million, over 30 per cent in one year.
The corporation has outperformed many of our leading industrial corporations. While it is true, that historically periodic fluctuations exist, with patterns of iean and fat years,
nonetheless the over-all picture, when viewed over a five-year period is one that the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation and all Canadians can be proud of. Sales have increased nearly 50 per cent, net income has increased by nearly 80 per cent, and retained earnings by nearly 120 per cent.
Today, the industry enjoys buoyant markets as the demand for fish expands. Yet the traditional cyclical nature of the industry will present the fishermen with new challenges.
The freshwater fisheries are now in transition. New technologies, especially the development of aquaculture, will see the introduction of a whole new interplay of market forces, in an arena in which an isolated fisherman would be at the mercy of these macroforces.
In conclusion, the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation is a success story of which we can all be proud. This is not to suggest that it is perfect, but we should consider that to change its mandate at this moment would return us to a position of relative weakness in an uncertain and fluctuating market.
For these reasons, and in recognition of the many successes it has had in a highly competitive and uncertain market-place, I believe that we should encourage and enhance the successes of this corporation.

Mr. Speaker, my subject tonight arises out of a question I put to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). It was in connection with the linkage between overseas aid and human rights, focusing particularly on the situation in Ethiopia, a country that has received both aid and development assistance from Canada in rich measure, but which has a shocking, indefensible human rights record, judged by the World Human Rights Guide, published by The Economist, as the worst in the world.
CIDA announced as of October 26 that Canada will give $10 million in food aid for drought stricken areas in Ethiopia which will bring to $20 million the total bilateral aid given to Ethiopia by CIDA, a previous $10 million having been divided equally among Government relief agencies and Canadian NGOs, non-governmental organizations. This is right. I join the Government in this with great enthusiasm and great commitment.
But I bring to the attention of the House two matters. The first concerns reports of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade and the response of the Government to that report. In the first instance, the standing committee of this House argues that human rights and overseas development assistance should always go together. The report of that committee, after an exhaustive study, stated that respect for human rights is one of the most important conditions for a true developmental process. It is not unreasonable therefore for Canada to expect that Governments receiving our aid will pursue approaches to development and in supporting human rights that can be broadly supported and approved by the Canadian people.
According to the standing committee, the Government should clearly base its decisions on aid and assistance on a set of principles that respect the priority of human rights. The Government has largely agreed with this contention of our standing committee. It has suggested in its response that the basic principle of the Government will be to ensure that repressive regimes are not legitimized through Canadian development assistance policy and that victims of human rights violations are not doubly penalized by being deprived of needed outside help as well as of their rights. I welcome the news that as far as Canadian aid will go, we will see to it that Ethiopians are not deprived of their human right to sustenance. But are we taking equal efforts to see that the people of Ethiopia are not deprived of their basic human rights, civil, political and social?
The Government has already said in its response that human rights concerns must be fully integrated into Canada's development policies. It has given us the advice that the most valuable guide to human rights is to focus on those violations which are patently systematic, gross and continuous. Clearly, the Government is overlooking, ignoring, bypassing, the patent systematic, gross and continuous violations of human rights in
Adjournment Debate
Ethiopia if the Government does not join together with its new and renewed aid programs an equally strong and, hopefully, successful emphasis upon human rights and the need of the Ethiopian Government to come up to at least minimum standards.
According to The Economist human rights guide, Ethiopia is worthy of a rating of only 13 per cent, by far the lowest in the world, and the lowest in Africa. There is no country in the world, according to this guide, that has a worse human rights record. Just listen, Mr. Speaker, to some of the human rights abuses in that sorry country. There is no freedom to travel in or outside the country. There is no freedom to peacefully associate. There is no freedom to exchange ideas and receive information. There is no freedom to publish and educate in ethnic languages.
As well, there are such shameful unbelievable abuses as these: serfdom, slavery, enforced and child labour, extrajudicial killings and disappearances, torture by the state, compulsory membership in state organizations, political censorship of the press, censorship of mail, no peaceful political opposition allowed, no rights for women, arbitrary police powers exercised and an arbitrary seizure of personal property.
The most flagrant abuse of human rights on the mass scale was as recent as this summer when the spectre of famine returned to the north of Ethiopia once again, not only because of drought but more particularly this time because of swarms of locusts attacking in massive numbers, seven huge swarms sweeping over Tigre and other parts of the land. Airplanes that could have carried spray to destroy those locusts were prevented from taking off at Addis Ababa. As the House may be informed, more recently aerial sprays have been permitted, but the delay has been a tragic human cost.
I urge that the Government use this opportunity of Ethiopia's need for food assistance and in rightful response to that need by the Canadian Government to insist and demand in the name of humanity that the Ethiopian Government give at least a minimal response to this plea for justice.

PHARMACEUTICAL INDUSTRY-BILL C-22-SENATE COMMITTEE'S REPORT/MINISTER'S POSITION

Mr. Speaker, on October 22, 1987, I posed a question to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) regarding the passage of Bill C-22 in the Upper Chamber whereby several amendments were made.
It should be noted that the debate on this particular subject matter has gone on for an extended period of time. My colleagues in the Upper Chamber have very reluctantly accepted the major thrust of Bill C-22. However, in order to clarify a number of points that had been made previously, particularly in lieu of the statements made by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and other Ministers of the Crown, across the country, the members of the Upper Chamber have made three amendments which in no way detract from the over-all thrust and substance of the Government's legislation.
In fact, the Upper Chamber has called for amendments with regard to job guarantees, expenditures on research and development, as well as guarantees with regard to consumer protection. Those three amendments would merely confirm in legislation what the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has been telling Canadians for many weeks, indeed months. In some respects it seems rather shameful that the Minister has not seen fit to concur with the reasonable amendments which have been made by members of the Upper Chamber.
I should point out for your edification, Mr. Speaker, that if these amendments were included in the legislation, they would provide a great deal of certainty and confidence to Canadians who, up until this point in time, have had some rather grave and serious reservations about the over-all thrust of Bill C-22.
I have asked the Minister to reflect upon and reconsider his point of view, not to object to or cast out of hand the obvious
reasonable amendments which have been made by the Upper Chamber.
In summary once again, the amendments moved by the Upper Chamber do not in any way derogate from the over-all thrust of the Government's legislation. They are an attempt to codify into law the statements which have been made by Canadians and organizations that travelled across the country to appear before the committee of the House of Commons and the committee of the Senate. It would codify those things which the Minister and the Government have been telling us about expenditures on research and development. I think all Canadians, indeed all Members of Parliament, would want to see them realized. Equally important would be the job guarantees to which our government colleagues have alluded. I hope they would see their way clear to reflecting upon these obviously reasonable yet important amendments to the over-all thrust of Bill C-22.
If the Minister wishes to be true to his word-and thousands of Canadians have heard him in the Chamber and across the country-he should have no difficulty whatsoever in placing the amendments into legislation and thereby accepting the principles laid down by the Upper Chamber and by Canadians from coast to coast, whether they be the United Church, senior citizens, provincial Governments, or whomever.
I hope the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister would reflect most sincerely on these very worth-while and reasonable amendments.

AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT-MINISTER'S POSITION ON FUNDING OF FANTASYLAND PROJECT-REASON FOR FUNDING PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my intention is to follow up on a question which pertains to the city from which you come. I know it will be of some interest to you. It has to do with the questions that I asked in the House last week of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) concerning a grant to the Fantasyland project in the Edmonton mall.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that when it was first raised the Deputy Prime Minister defended the decision to give the money to the Fantasyland project on the basis of how, in his judgment, he thought that the project was good for Edmonton, the mall and western Canada. We were quarreling about whether the criterion for selecting which project would get these moneys had been met and whether the Deputy Prime Minister had bent or broken the rules in order to provide the grant.
The Deputy Prime Minister in the early stages of the debate last week did not even try to pretend that the criterion had been met. He argued that what he had done was the right thing on the basis of what he thought to be the merits of the project regardless of the criterion. It was only in subsequent days that he then started to try to find ways in which he could fit the Fantasyland project into the criterion. It was interesting to see this line of argument develop over the next few days.
I want to address myself to some of the rhetoric that accompanied the defence by the Deputy Prime Minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) of the Government's decision to give this money to the Fantasyland project. What I object to strongly, and I hope you share this view, Mr. Speaker, is that Members of Parliament should be able to rise-opposition Members in this case-and ask legitimate questions of the Deputy Prime Minister or any other Member of the Cabinet about the granting of moneys to particular projects without having to be subject to the accusation that
Adjournment Debate
because we raise a question we are against a region, in this case western Canada.
I hope that some day western Canadians like myself can ask another western Canadian, in this case the Deputy Prime Minister, without having either the Deputy Prime Minister or the Prime Minister say, as the Prime Minister did say on the record, that the NDP is somehow against the interests of western Canada because we raised an issue. If we raise an issue with respect to some contract given in Atlantic Canada, are we against the interests of Atlantic Canada? If we raise an issue with respect to the granting of a contract in Quebec, are we against the interests of Quebec? If you cannot raise these kinds of issues without that kind of accusation being leveled, you cannot do your job.
I think it was a very low point in the life of Parliament when that kind of an accusation was made against myself and against other New Democrats because we raised such a question. I can tell you sincerely that this kind of regional McCarthyism, or as we have called it, regional racism, has the same dynamic that whenever you raise a question you are accused of something. Conservative Members of Parliament in previous Parliaments used to be frustrated when they asked a question about something happening in Quebec and Liberal Cabinet Ministers of those days used to retort, no matter what the question was, "You are against Quebec". Conservative Members of Parliament did not think that was an appropriate response by Cabinet Ministers then and it is not an appropriate response today when the Deputy Prime Minister or the Prime Minister use that kind of an answer to respond to that kind of a question by Members of Parliament.
Western Canada is a politically plural society. There is more than one political tradition in western Canada. Conservatives need to have enough respect for western Canada to realize it is not just Conservatives who speak for western Canada. With respect to many controversial western issues, whether it be energy policy or whatever the case may be, there are one or more views.
The tradition from which I speak, the CCF and NDP tradition, actually predates in many respects the tradition of the Deputy Prime Minister. He is basically a product of the Conservative tradition in western Canada created by John Diefenbaker. Long before John Diefenbaker came along, there were CCF members who spoke out for western Canada.
Many Canadians resent this monopoly that western Progressive Conservatives think they have on speaking for western Canada. It will come back to haunt them because western Canadians do not appreciate those who think they have a monopoly on their particular political mind-set. I think we saw that developing out of the events that happened here last week and out of what I understand to be some of the comments made about the exchanges that took place in the House last week.

November 2, 1987
Adjournment Debate
I make a sincere appeal as one Member of Parliament to other Members of Parliament, let us not drag this place down by getting into this game of accusing each other of being against any particular region or in this case, against western Canada. My children are the fourth generation of my family to have made their homes in western Canada and I for one will just not put up with somebody like the Deputy Prime Minister saying that I am against western Canada. It is not true and the Deputy Prime Minister should have more respect for Parliament and for other Hon. Members than to have suggested that.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Hon. Member's colleague from Skeena might take heed of the very apt and appropriate words he has just directed to us. For the record, it should be of interest to the Hon. Member to be aware of what DRIE officials actually had to say about this particular transaction. I wish to quote from a response DRIE officials made to the Auditor General last summer:
-that the application for assistance for this project was received on December 7, 1983 and while tourism was dropped from IRDP on November 9, 1984, the application was protected under the grandfather provision. It is clear from file documentation that the necessary permits, construction contracts and
actual construction on this project was/were not entered into prior to December 7, 1983 and therefore the project was not prior committed within the terms of Section 29(1) of the pre-November 9, 1984 regulations to the IRDP. DRIE's position remains that the project continued to be eligible for assistance consideration under IRDP, notwithstanding the fact that construction was well advanced in August, 1985 when the DRIE Minister made the actual decision to assist... The IRDP contribution facilitated the company in arranging the additional financing and consequently ensured that the project was completed within the originally proposed scope and timing. If DRIE had not offered the assistance at that time, it is highly probably that construction would have been delayed and the significant contributions that have accrued to Canada's economy over the past two years from this tourism facility would have been substantially lessened.
That is the position of DRIE. Obviously the Auditor General has the right to examine it, to consider whether or not it was appropriate and indeed to reject it, but the fact remains that that was the position of DRIE acknowledged by the Auditor General.
